body:
Resistance turns energy into heat and is the same at every frequency. Reactance stores and releases energy instead. A capacitor's reactance falls as frequency rises (Xc = 1/2πfC), and an inductor's rises (XL = 2πfL). Impedance (Z) is the combination of the two. That is why a single number on a spec sheet is only a 'nominal' value: an 8 Ω loudspeaker can dip close to 3 Ω in one band and rise well above 30 Ω at its bass resonance.

Modern audio connects equipment by voltage bridging, not impedance matching. A low source impedance drives an input with a much higher impedance, roughly ten times or more, so nearly all the signal voltage arrives. A dynamic mic of about 150–300 Ω feeds a preamp input of about 1.5–3 kΩ. A line output of around 100 Ω feeds an input of 10 kΩ or more. A power amp's output impedance is a small fraction of an ohm against a 4–8 Ω speaker. Matching 600 Ω to 600 Ω comes from telephone lines and old broadcast practice, where very long lines and power transfer mattered. It is rarely what you want today.

Impedance becomes audible when that rule is broken. A guitar pickup has a high, inductive source impedance, so plugged into a 10 kΩ line input it loses level and top end. That is why it needs a Hi-Z input of about 1 MΩ or a DI. A high source impedance driving a long cable forms a low-pass filter with the cable's capacitance. Ribbon and some dynamic mics change tone with preamp input impedance, which is why some preamps let you switch it. A headphone amp with high output impedance changes the frequency response of headphones whose impedance varies with frequency.
inPractice: On your next session with a dynamic or ribbon mic, switch the preamp's input impedance (if it has the option) and listen to the low end and presence change. When a bass or keyboard sounds dull through a line input, put it through a DI before you reach for EQ.
keyPoints: Impedance = resistance + reactance; it varies with frequency, measured in ohms.
Bridging: low-impedance outputs into inputs about 10× higher or more. Don't 'match' unless a spec says so.
Nominal speaker and headphone impedances are averages; the real curve swings widely.
High-Z sources (guitar pickups, piezos) need about 1 MΩ inputs or a DI box.
Keep source impedance low when driving long cables, or the cable capacitance rolls off the highs.
mistake: Thinking impedances must be 'matched'. Into a 600 Ω load, a modern line output loses level and may distort. What matters is that the input impedance is well above the output impedance.
sayIt: Impedance is how hard a circuit pushes back against an audio signal; we keep outputs low and inputs high so the signal arrives without losing level or tone.
summary: Impedance is the total opposition a circuit offers to an alternating signal, measured in ohms (Ω). It combines plain resistance with reactance from capacitance and inductance, so unlike resistance it changes with frequency.

terms.def: Frequency-dependent opposition from capacitance or inductance, in ohms.
Connecting a low-impedance output to a much higher-impedance input so voltage transfers almost fully.
High-impedance input (about 1 MΩ) for instruments with passive pickups.
Load impedance divided by the amplifier's output impedance (plus cable); how well the amp controls the driver.
A single representative figure for a component whose real impedance varies with frequency.

title: Impedance, explained properly

body:
Sampling takes a snapshot of the voltage fs times a second. At 48 kHz that is every 20.8 microseconds. The sampling theorem (Nyquist–Shannon) says that if the input is band-limited below fs/2, those snapshots hold all the information, and an ideal reconstruction filter rebuilds the original waveform exactly, not an approximation. So 44.1 kHz covers content up to 22.05 kHz and 48 kHz up to 24 kHz, both above the roughly 20 kHz limit of young human hearing.

The condition matters. A component above Nyquist produces exactly the same samples as one below it, so the converter cannot tell them apart. It appears at |f − n·fs|, the distance to the nearest multiple of the sample rate. A 30 kHz tone sampled at 48 kHz lands at 18 kHz, and a 40 kHz tone lands at 8 kHz. Aliases are not harmonically related to the source, so they sound like dirty, inharmonic tones that move the wrong way when the pitch moves. That is why every ADC has an anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the sampling stage, and every DAC has a reconstruction filter after it. Modern delta-sigma converters sample at a very high internal rate and use steep digital filters to bring the rate down, which is how they get flat response close to 20 kHz.

The problem returns inside the computer. Anything nonlinear, such as saturation, clipping, fast limiting or FM synthesis, creates new harmonics, and some of them land above Nyquist and fold back. Oversampling runs the process at two to sixteen times the rate, filters off the excess and comes back down. The cost is CPU and a little latency, like the 16 samples Apogee's Soft Limit adds at any oversampling setting. Linear processes such as gain, EQ and most reverbs create no new frequencies, so they have no aliasing to remove, although some EQs oversample to keep their curves accurate near Nyquist.

Higher session rates have practical uses. At 96 kHz, recordings keep content up to 48 kHz, so sound designers can pitch them down an octave and still fill the audible band. Film and TV work at 48 kHz because that is the video standard. Whatever the rate, check that content above about 20 kHz is not hitting IEMs, tweeters or a later process that will fold it back.
inPractice: Put a sine sweep from 1 kHz to 20 kHz through your favourite saturation plugin at 48 kHz with oversampling off, and watch a spectrum analyser: aliases show up as tones that fall while the sweep rises. Turn oversampling on and compare, then decide where it is worth the CPU in your template.
keyPoints: Nyquist frequency = fs / 2: 22.05 kHz at 44.1 kHz, 24 kHz at 48 kHz.
Content above Nyquist folds back to |f − n·fs|: 30 kHz at 48 kHz becomes 18 kHz.
Anti-aliasing filters before the ADC and reconstruction filters after the DAC are part of every converter.
Nonlinear plugins create harmonics that can alias; oversampling reduces this at a CPU and latency cost.
Properly reconstructed digital audio is a smooth waveform, not a staircase.
mistake: Many people think samples make a stepped 'staircase' that higher rates smooth out. The reconstruction filter rebuilds a smooth waveform, and a higher rate only extends the bandwidth; it does not make audible content more accurate.
sayIt: Digital audio captures everything below half the sample rate perfectly, and anything above that has to be filtered out first or it comes back as false tones lower down.
summary: A digital system measures the signal at a fixed rate, the sample rate fs. The sampling theorem says a signal can be rebuilt exactly if it contains nothing at or above half that rate, the Nyquist frequency fs/2. Anything above Nyquist does not disappear: it folds back into the audio band as aliasing.

terms.def: How many times per second the signal is measured, e.g. 48,000 Hz.
Half the sample rate; the highest frequency a system can represent.
Content above Nyquist that folds back into the audio band as a false frequency.
A low-pass filter that removes content above Nyquist before sampling.
Running a process at a multiple of the sample rate so new harmonics stay below the raised Nyquist, then filtering and converting back.

title: Sampling, Nyquist and aliasing

The EU and NIOSH treat damage as proportional to sound energy. A 3 dB rise doubles the energy, so it halves the safe time. This is the 3 dB exchange rate, or equal-energy rule. NIOSH recommends 85 dB(A) for 8 hours, which gives 88 dB(A) for 4 hours, 91 for 2 hours, 94 for 1 hour, 97 for 30 minutes and 100 for 15 minutes. The US OSHA legal limit uses 90 dB(A) for 8 hours with a 5 dB exchange rate. That is far more lenient at high levels: OSHA allows 100 dB(A) for 2 hours, while NIOSH allows only 15 minutes.

To get LEX,8h from a measured level, use LEX,8h = LAeq,T + 10·log10(T / 8 h). Two hours at 94 dB(A) gives 94 + 10·log10(0.25) = 94 − 6 = 88 dB(A). Noise dose is the same idea expressed as a percentage: dose = (actual time / allowed time) × 100. Four hours at 91 dB(A) under NIOSH is 4 / 2 = 200%. Doses from different parts of the day add up: half your allowance at FOH plus half on a loud stage makes 100%.

In the EU, Directive 2003/10/EC sets three thresholds (Italy uses the same values in D.Lgs. 81/2008). At the lower action value of 80 dB(A) LEX,8h or 135 dB(C) peak, the employer must provide information and make hearing protection available. At the upper action value of 85 dB(A) or 137 dB(C) peak, protection must be worn and a noise-reduction programme is required. The exposure limit value of 87 dB(A) or 140 dB(C) peak must never be exceeded at the ear, and this is the one value that takes the protector's attenuation into account. For audiences, the WHO Global Standard for Safe Listening Venues and Events (2022) sets 100 dB LAeq over any 15 minutes.

In practice, a mixer standing at 98 dB(A) at FOH reaches 85 dB(A) LEX,8h in about 25 minutes. Earplugs only help if they fit. The SNR or NRR printed on the box is measured in a lab with an ideal fit, and real-world attenuation is often much lower. Flat-response musicians' plugs with custom moulds, IEMs at controlled levels, and taking breaks during soundcheck are what keep your dose down. Damage can also happen without a lasting change in the audiogram: animal studies show noise can destroy the synapses between hair cells and nerve fibres even after the threshold recovers.
inPractice: At your next show, run a free SPL app or a meter with LAeq at your mix position for the full set. Compute your LEX,8h with the formula above, then add the soundcheck time and see how much of your daily allowance you used.
keyPoints: 3 dB exchange rate: every +3 dB halves the allowed time
LEX,8h = LAeq,T + 10·log10(T / 8 h)
EU and Italy: 80 dB(A) lower action, 85 upper action, 87 limit (at the ear, with protection)
Peak thresholds: 135, 137 and 140 dB(C)
Dose % = actual time / allowed time × 100, and doses across the day add up
Labelled SNR/NRR is a lab figure; real-world fit usually gives less
mistake: Many people think 85 dB(A) is a hard line that is safe below and dangerous above. It is an 8-hour average. Ninety minutes at 92 dB(A) is already well over, and short periods below 85 don't cancel out loud ones.
sayIt: Hearing damage depends on how loud it is and for how long. Every 3 dB louder halves the time you can safely spend there.
summary: Noise damage depends on the total sound energy reaching the ear over time, not on level alone. Exposure rules convert a working day's noise into one number, the daily noise exposure level LEX,8h: the steady A-weighted level that would deliver the same energy over 8 hours. Each regulation sets action values and limits against that number.

terms.def: Daily noise exposure level: the steady A-weighted level that would give the same sound energy over an 8-hour working day.
Equivalent continuous A-weighted sound level over a period T, an energy average.
How many dB increase halves the allowed exposure time: 3 dB under the EU and NIOSH, 5 dB under OSHA.
Highest instantaneous C-weighted sound pressure level, used for impulse limits such as 135, 137 and 140 dB(C).
Single-number attenuation ratings for hearing protectors, measured in the lab (SNR in the EU, NRR in the US).
Loss of synapses between inner hair cells and auditory nerve fibres after noise, which can occur without a lasting threshold shift.

title: Noise dose: exchange rates, LEX,8h and exposure limits

At low frequencies most monitors radiate almost equally in all directions, so energy goes backwards as well as forwards. That energy hits the front wall behind the speaker and comes back towards you. For a listener on axis, the reflected path is about twice the distance d from the speaker's acoustic centre to the wall, so the reflection arrives with a delay of 2d/c. Where that extra path equals half a wavelength, the two waves are out of phase and cancel. The first and deepest cancellation is at f = c / (4d). With c = 343 m/s, a speaker 1 m from the wall has its first null near 86 Hz; at 0.5 m it moves to about 172 Hz; at 2 m it falls to about 43 Hz. Further nulls follow at 3, 5, 7… times that frequency, getting shallower because the reflection is weaker at higher frequencies.

The same thing happens with every nearby boundary: side walls, the floor and the desk. Each distance gives its own null, and when two distances are similar, the dips pile up in one region. At very low frequencies, where the wall is much less than a quarter wavelength away, the reflection adds in phase instead, giving boundary gain of up to about +6 dB per boundary in theory. This is why monitors have 'half space', 'quarter space' or bass-tilt switches.

You cannot fix an SBIR null with EQ. Boosting the frequency raises the direct and reflected sound equally, so they still cancel, and you only spend amplifier and driver headroom. The fixes are geometric. Move the speaker very close to the wall, so the first null moves above the woofer's working range, or flush-mount it so there is no gap at all. Alternatively, move it far enough away that the null falls below the range the speaker reproduces strongly, or use a subwoofer placed near the wall with a crossover chosen to avoid the null. Thick porous absorption behind the speaker helps only if it is deep enough; a panel needs to approach a quarter wavelength in depth to be effective, which at 86 Hz is about 1 m.

SBIR is easy to measure. Put a measurement mic at the listening position, sweep one speaker at a time, and look for a dip whose frequency moves when you move the speaker. In post rooms, height and surround speakers close to walls and ceilings show the same effect, and so do PA subs placed near a stage wall.
inPractice: Measure one monitor at your mix position with REW or similar, then move it 20 cm closer to the wall and measure again. Note how the low-frequency dip moves, and pick the position where it does the least damage before you touch any EQ.
keyPoints: First SBIR null: f = c / (4d), with d from the acoustic centre to the boundary.
1 m from the wall gives about 86 Hz; 0.5 m gives about 172 Hz.
Further nulls fall at 3, 5, 7 × that frequency and get shallower.
EQ cannot fill an SBIR null; it only wastes headroom.
Fix it with placement: very close, flush-mounted or far from the boundary.
SBIR dips move when the speaker moves; room modes do not.
mistake: Many people boost the missing bass with room-correction EQ. A cancellation is a timing problem, not a level problem, so the boost does not help and can push the woofer into distortion.
sayIt: The wall behind your speakers sends some of the bass back late enough to cancel itself out, so a certain band disappears at your chair, and moving the speakers is the only real cure.
summary: Speaker-boundary interference is the comb-filter pattern created when sound from a loudspeaker reflects off a nearby wall, floor or desk and combines with the direct sound at the listening position. The delayed reflection cancels the direct sound at frequencies where it arrives half a wavelength late, producing a deep dip in the low-frequency response that depends on the distance to the boundary.

terms.def: Speaker-boundary interference response: the comb filtering caused by reflections from boundaries close to a loudspeaker.
The point from which a loudspeaker's sound appears to radiate at a given frequency; used to measure distances for SBIR and alignment.
The low-frequency level increase when a source is close to a boundary and its reflection adds in phase, up to about +6 dB per boundary in theory.
Building the speaker into the wall so its front baffle is level with the wall surface, removing the rear-wall reflection gap.
A frequency response with regularly spaced peaks and dips, caused by adding a signal to a delayed copy of itself.

title: Speaker-boundary interference (SBIR)

body:
A compressor has two parts: a detector that measures level and a gain computer that decides how much to turn down. Above the threshold, a hard-knee compressor's output rises by 1 dB for every R dB of input, where R is the ratio. Gain reduction is therefore (input − threshold) × (1 − 1/R). A peak 12 dB over the threshold at 4:1 comes out 3 dB over, so it is reduced by 9 dB.

Attack and release are time constants, not fixed delays. In most designs, gain reduction moves exponentially towards its target, and the quoted time is how long it takes to get most of the way there; manufacturers define this differently, so the same '10 ms' does not sound identical on two units. Typical ranges show the spread: a classic FET design such as the 1176 attacks in 20–800 microseconds, while the SSL-style bus compressor offers 0.1 to 30 ms attack and 0.1 to 1.2 s release plus Auto. Program-dependent or auto release recovers quickly after short peaks and more slowly after sustained ones.

Time constants interact with frequency. A 50 Hz waveform has a 20 ms period. If attack and release are only a few milliseconds, the gain changes within each cycle and reshapes the waveform itself, which adds harmonic distortion. That can be useful as an effect, but on bass, kick or a full mix it usually sounds grainy. Slower attack lets the transient through before the gain comes down, which is why a 10–30 ms attack on a drum bus makes the hits punchier.

Detection matters as much. A peak detector reacts to the highest instantaneous values and is good for catching transients. An RMS detector averages the signal's power over a window, so it reacts more like the ear does to loudness and gives smoother control on vocals and mixes. Many units also put a high-pass filter in the side-chain so low frequencies don't drive the gain reduction, which stops a mix bus pumping with the kick.
inPractice: On a drum bus, set 4:1 and about 6 dB of gain reduction, then sweep attack from fastest to 30 ms while watching the meter and listening to the snare crack. Set release so the gain-reduction meter returns close to zero just before the next beat.
keyPoints: Gain reduction = (input − threshold) × (1 − 1/ratio) for a hard knee.
Attack and release are time constants; definitions differ between manufacturers.
Time constants shorter than a waveform's period distort low frequencies.
Slower attack lets transients through and adds punch.
RMS detection follows loudness; peak detection catches transients.
A side-chain HPF stops bass from driving the compressor.
mistake: Many people think a faster attack is always more controlled and therefore better. It also removes the transient that gives a sound its definition, and on bass it adds distortion; choose attack to keep or remove the transient on purpose.
sayIt: Attack and release decide how fast the compressor reacts and lets go, and that timing is what makes it sound punchy, smooth or squashed.
summary: Attack and release set how quickly a compressor's gain reduction responds when the signal rises above and falls back below the threshold. The detector decides what level the compressor reacts to, from instantaneous peaks to an average over a time window, and together these settings shape the sound far more than the ratio does.

terms.def: The level above which the compressor starts reducing gain.
How gradually the ratio changes around the threshold; a soft knee blends compression in over a range of levels.
Measuring level as an average of signal power over a short window, closer to perceived loudness.
A release time that changes with the material, faster after brief peaks and slower after sustained loud passages.
The signal path that feeds the detector, which can be filtered or taken from another source.

title: Compressor attack, release and detection

K-weighting is two filters in series: a high shelf of about +4 dB in the upper frequencies, which models the acoustic effect of the head, and a high-pass (the RLB curve) that rolls off the low bass. The filtered signal of each channel is squared and averaged. Left, right and centre have a weight of 1.0, the surrounds 1.41 (about +1.5 dB), and the LFE channel is not counted. The weighted powers are added and converted to a logarithmic value. As a reference point, a 0 dBFS 1 kHz sine in one front channel reads −3.01 LUFS.

The same calculation runs over different time windows. Momentary loudness uses a 400 ms window, short-term uses 3 s. Integrated loudness covers the whole programme but is gated: it uses 400 ms blocks overlapping by 75%, discards blocks below −70 LUFS (the absolute gate), measures the rest, then discards blocks more than 10 LU below that result (the relative gate) and measures again. Gating stops silence and quiet passages from dragging the number down.

Loudness Range (EBU Tech 3342) describes how much the loudness varies. It takes the short-term values, applies an absolute gate at −70 LUFS and a relative gate 20 LU below, and reports the difference between the 10th and 95th percentiles of what remains. Ignoring the quietest 10% and the loudest 5% keeps a single fade-out or explosion from dominating. True peak is a separate measurement: the signal is oversampled (four times at 48 kHz) so that peaks between samples, which can appear after conversion or lossy encoding, are caught.

Targets: EBU R128 asks for −23 LUFS integrated (±0.5 LU, ±1 LU for live) and a maximum of −1 dBTP. ATSC A/85 in the US uses −24 LKFS with −2 dBTP. Netflix measures dialogue-gated loudness at −27 LKFS. In film and TV post the integrated number is the pass or fail figure, LRA tells you whether the mix will sit well on a television, and true peak protects the encoder.
inPractice: Bounce a finished mix, measure it in two different meters, and write down integrated loudness, LRA and true peak from each. Then remove the LFE channel from a 5.1 mix and check that the integrated figure does not change.
keyPoints: LUFS and LKFS are the same unit; 1 LU = 1 dB.
K-weighting: +4 dB high shelf plus a low-bass high-pass; LFE is not measured.
Momentary 400 ms, short-term 3 s, integrated is gated (−70 LUFS, then −10 LU).
LRA = 95th minus 10th percentile of gated short-term loudness.
R128: −23 LUFS, −1 dBTP. A/85: −24 LKFS, −2 dBTP.
Measure the bounced file, and use true peak, not sample peak.
mistake: Many people think a quiet intro or a long silence lowers the integrated reading enough to let the rest run hot. Gating discards silence and very quiet blocks, so the loud sections largely set the number.
sayIt: A loudness meter measures how loud the whole programme feels on average, weighted the way our ears hear, so every broadcast sits at the same level and nobody reaches for the remote.
summary: Loudness meters following ITU-R BS.1770 filter the signal with K-weighting, take the mean-square power of each channel, apply channel weights, sum, and express the result in LUFS (LKFS), where 1 LU equals 1 dB. EBU R128 and ATSC A/85 build delivery targets on that measurement, using gating for integrated loudness and a statistical measure (LRA) for loudness range.

terms.def: Loudness Units relative to Full Scale; the absolute loudness unit of BS.1770. The two names mean the same thing.
The frequency weighting used by BS.1770: a high shelf plus a low-frequency high-pass.
Leaving out measurement blocks below a threshold so that silence and quiet passages do not lower the integrated value.
Loudness Range, defined in EBU Tech 3342: the spread between the 10th and 95th percentiles of gated short-term loudness, in LU.
Decibels true peak: the peak level measured after oversampling, catching inter-sample peaks.

title: How a loudness meter actually measures

body:
Take a delay of t seconds between two copies of the same signal. A frequency cancels when the delay equals half its period, or any odd number of half periods. So the notches fall at f = (2n − 1) / (2t): the first at 1/(2t), then every 1/t above that. With 1 ms of delay, the notches sit at 500 Hz, 1.5 kHz, 2.5 kHz and so on, 1 kHz apart. Sound travels about 343 m/s at 20 °C, so 1 ms is about 34 cm of path difference. Two mics on one source with a 34 cm difference in distance give you exactly that comb.

How deep the notches go depends on the level difference between the two copies. At equal level, the peaks reach +6 dB and the notches cancel completely. If the second copy is 6 dB down (half the amplitude), the peaks are 20·log(1.5) ≈ +3.5 dB and the notches 20·log(0.5) = −6 dB. At about 10 dB down, the ripple shrinks to roughly +2.5 dB and −3.5 dB. This is why the 3:1 rule works: keep the second mic at least three times farther from a source than that source's own mic, and the inverse square law drops the spill by about 9.5 dB.

Flipping polarity does not remove comb filtering. It multiplies every frequency by −1, so the peaks and notches swap places. With 1 ms of delay and one copy inverted, the notches move to 0 Hz, 1 kHz, 2 kHz and so on, which means the low end cancels. The polarity switch helps when the offset is small compared with the wavelengths you care about, such as kick in and kick out, or snare top and bottom. Only delay can actually line up two arrivals in time.

You will hear this everywhere. You get it with overheads against close drum mics, a DI against a miked bass cab, a boom against a lav on the same actor, a desk reflection into a talk mic, and a delay speaker that is out of time with the main PA. In post, a lav sitting about 30 cm closer than the boom gives roughly 0.9 ms of offset. Sliding one track by that amount, or with a time-alignment plugin, often helps more than any EQ.
inPractice: On the next drum or dialogue session, zoom in on a transient in the close mic and the distant mic, measure the offset in samples, and slide the distant mic to match. Solo both, compare aligned and unaligned, and listen for the low mids coming back.
keyPoints: First notch at 1/(2t); notches repeat every 1/t.
1 ms ≈ 34 cm of path at 343 m/s.
Equal levels: +6 dB peaks, full cancellation at the notches.
A 10 dB level difference cuts the ripple to a few dB, which is why the 3:1 rule works.
Polarity swaps peaks and notches; only delay aligns arrivals.
Measure the offset on the waveform, then nudge by samples.
mistake: People often assume the polarity button fixes 'phase problems' between any two mics. It only inverts the signal. For mics at different distances it moves the comb to different frequencies, and a time shift is the real fix.
sayIt: When two mics hear the same sound at slightly different times, some frequencies cancel, so we line them up in time before we touch the EQ.
summary: Comb filtering happens when a signal is added to a delayed copy of itself. Frequencies whose delayed copy arrives in phase are reinforced, and those that arrive half a cycle late cancel. The result is a run of evenly spaced peaks and notches whose positions depend only on the delay time.

terms.def: A frequency response with evenly spaced peaks and notches, caused by adding a signal to a delayed copy of itself.
The sign of the signal. Inverting it multiplies the waveform by −1 at every frequency, with no time shift.
The position within a cycle at a given frequency. A time delay produces a phase shift that grows with frequency.
Keep the distance between mics at least three times each mic's distance to its own source, so spill is about 9.5 dB down.
Delaying the earlier signal so that both arrivals line up, removing the comb caused by the offset.

title: Comb filtering and mic time alignment

Timecode comes in standard frame rates: 24, 25 (the European broadcast rate), 30, and the NTSC-derived 23.976 and 29.97, which run 1000/1001 slower than 24 and 30. Longitudinal timecode (LTC) carries the address as an audio-band signal: an 80-bit word per frame, biphase-mark encoded so polarity doesn't matter. At 25 fps that is 80 × 25 = 2,000 bits per second. In a Broadcast WAV file, the start time is stored in the bext chunk's TimeReference field as a count of samples since midnight. iXML metadata usually carries the frame rate and other details alongside it.

At 29.97 fps, a frame counter that counts a full 30 frames per second falls behind the wall clock by about 3.6 seconds per hour. Drop-frame timecode fixes this by skipping frame numbers 00 and 01 at the start of every minute, except every tenth minute. That is 2 × 54 = 108 numbers per hour, matching the 108 frames of drift. No frames of picture are dropped, only labels. Drop-frame is written with a semicolon before the frames (01:00:00;00). Mixing DF and NDF on one job shifts sync further and further as time goes on.

Because timecode is only an address, two devices jammed to the same time will still drift apart if their clocks run at slightly different rates. A clock error of 1 ppm is 3.6 ms per hour. Over a 12-hour day that is about 43 ms, slightly more than one frame at 25 fps (40 ms). This is why sync boxes quote accuracy in ppm, why you re-jam at lunch on long days with older gear, and why a camera that only reads timecode at the start of a take can slip over a long interview. Locking the recorder's sample clock to a common reference (genlock, word clock, or a sync box that disciplines the sample rate) stops the drift itself, rather than just relabelling it.

On set, agree the project frame rate and DF/NDF with post before day one. Use time-of-day timecode as free run so every device shares a reference, and log what each camera actually receives. Small cameras often share one input between timecode and a mic. In post, conform from the BWF TimeReference, not from file creation times, and check sync at the end of long takes as well as the start.
inPractice: Jam a recorder and a camera from the same sync box, roll both for an hour on a clap at the start and the end, then line up the start clap in your DAW and measure the offset at the end clap. That tells you how much the pair actually drifts and how often you need to re-jam.
keyPoints: Timecode is a frame address (HH:MM:SS:FF), not a speed reference.
LTC uses 80 bits per frame: 2,000 bit/s at 25 fps.
29.97 DF skips frame numbers 00 and 01 every minute except each tenth minute: 108 per hour.
1 ppm clock error = 3.6 ms per hour of drift.
BWF stores start time as samples since midnight in bext TimeReference.
Genlock or word clock stops drift; jamming only resets the address.
mistake: Many people think 'drop frame' means frames of picture or audio are thrown away. Only the frame numbers are skipped, to keep the displayed time in step with the clock. The media itself stays continuous.
sayIt: Timecode is like a street address stamped on every frame, so we can line things up later. It doesn't make the camera and recorder run at exactly the same speed, so on long days they can creep apart unless we re-jam or lock them to a common clock.
summary: SMPTE timecode (SMPTE ST 12) labels each video frame with an address in hours, minutes, seconds and frames (HH:MM:SS:FF). It tells devices where they are, so separately recorded picture and sound can be lined up later. It does not set how fast each device runs. That is the job of each device's internal crystal, or of an external reference such as genlock or word clock.

terms.def: Longitudinal timecode: timecode carried as a biphase-mark audio-band signal on a cable or audio track, 80 bits per frame.
A 29.97 fps counting scheme that skips frame numbers 00 and 01 each minute except every tenth, so displayed time matches real time.
Setting a device's timecode generator to match a master, after which it free-runs on its own clock.
Locking a device's frame or sample clock to an external reference so its running speed matches the master.
The Broadcast WAV field holding the file's start time as a sample count since midnight.

title: Timecode is an address, not a clock

body:
A pressure capsule is sealed at the back, so it responds to sound pressure from every direction equally: an omni, A = 1, B = 0. A pressure-gradient capsule is open on both sides and responds to the difference in pressure between front and back. That difference is largest for sound arriving on axis, zero for sound from the side and inverted in polarity from the rear, which gives the figure-8: A = 0, B = 1, r(θ) = cos θ, with nulls at 90° and 270°.

Mix the two and you get the cardioid family. A cardioid is 0.5 + 0.5·cos θ: full level at 0°, 0.5 (−6 dB) at 90° and a null at 180°. A supercardioid (about A = 0.37, B = 0.63) is −8.6 dB at the sides with nulls near 126°, and a small rear lobe about 11.7 dB down. A hypercardioid (A = 0.25, B = 0.75) is −12 dB at 90°, with nulls at about 110° and a rear lobe only 6 dB down. Setting cos θ = −A/B gives the null angle for any blend.

The pattern also decides how much diffuse room sound the mic hears. Relative to an omni, the random-energy efficiency is 1/3 for cardioid and figure-8 (about −4.8 dB), about 0.27 for supercardioid (−5.7 dB) and 0.25 for hypercardioid (−6 dB). The square root of the inverse gives the distance factor: a cardioid can be about 1.7 times as far away as an omni for the same direct-to-reverberant ratio, a hypercardioid about 2 times. This is why a hyper on a boom can work a little farther back than a cardioid in a reflective room.

Anything with a gradient component also has proximity effect: close to a source the spherical wavefront raises the pressure difference at low frequencies, so the bass rises as distance shrinks. A figure-8 shows it most, a cardioid less, and a pure pressure omni not at all. Real mics are only first-order in theory: most omnis become directional at high frequencies, and many cardioids widen in the bass, so off-axis sound is coloured, not just quieter. Multi-pattern condensers use two back-to-back cardioid diaphragms: one alone is cardioid, both summed in phase give omni, and both summed with one polarity inverted give figure-8.
inPractice: Put a speaker playing pink noise at 0°, 90°, 110° and 180° to a cardioid and a hypercardioid and compare levels and tone. Then aim your wedge or the noisy camera at the measured null, not just 'behind the mic'.
keyPoints: r(θ) = A + B·cos θ, with A + B = 1: A is the omni part, B the figure-8 part.
Cardioid: −6 dB at 90°, null at 180°. Hypercardioid: −12 dB at 90°, nulls near 110°, rear lobe −6 dB.
Null angle: cos θ = −A/B.
Distance factor vs omni: cardioid ≈ 1.7, supercardioid ≈ 1.9, hypercardioid ≈ 2.0.
Proximity effect comes from the gradient part: none on a pure omni, strongest on a figure-8.
Real patterns change with frequency, so off-axis sound is coloured as well as reduced.
mistake: Many people put a wedge directly behind a hypercardioid vocal mic, assuming the rear is the quietest point. A hyper's rear lobe is only about 6 dB down; its nulls are at roughly 110°, so wedges belong off to the sides of the rear.
sayIt: Every directional mic is a mix of an 'everything' mic and a 'front-and-back' mic, and the mix decides where it is deaf, how much room it hears and how much bass it adds up close.
summary: A first-order microphone's polar pattern is a blend of a pressure (omnidirectional) response and a pressure-gradient (figure-8) response, written as r(θ) = A + B·cos θ with A + B = 1. Changing the ratio of A to B moves you from omni through cardioid, supercardioid and hypercardioid to figure-8, and sets where the nulls fall, how much room sound the mic picks up and how strong its proximity effect is.

terms.def: A diaphragm sealed at the back that responds to pressure equally from all directions (omni).
Response to the pressure difference between the two sides of an open diaphragm; gives the figure-8.
How much diffuse, all-directions sound a mic picks up relative to an omni.
How much farther a directional mic can be placed than an omni for the same direct-to-reverberant ratio.
The low-frequency rise of gradient mics as the source gets close.

title: Polar patterns from first principles

body:
Any sound reinforcement system is a loop. The talker reaches the mic, the PA reproduces it, and part of the PA's output arrives back at the mic. If that returned sound is as loud as the original at some frequency, and in phase with it, the loop sustains itself and rings. Below that point the system still rings briefly after each word, which is why a system 'on the edge' sounds coloured and hollow even when it is not howling.

The classic estimate from Davis and Patronis uses four distances: Ds from talker to mic, D1 from mic to the nearest loudspeaker, D2 from that loudspeaker to the farthest listener, and D0 from talker to that listener. In a free field, PAG = 20·log(D0·D1 / (Ds·D2)) − 10·log(NOM) − FSM. NOM is the number of open microphones, and FSM is a feedback stability margin, usually 6 dB. NAG = 20·log(D0 / EAD), where EAD is the equivalent acoustic distance: how close the listener would have to stand to the unamplified talker to hear as well as they do with the system on. The design works only if PAG is at least NAG.

The formula shows where the decibels come from. Ds is the strongest lever: halving the talker-to-mic distance gains 6 dB, so going from 60 cm to 15 cm gains 12 dB. Moving the loudspeaker farther from the mic (larger D1) helps by the same law, and every doubling of open mics costs 3 dB. Directional mics and speakers add gain on top by rejecting the return path, which is why you aim a wedge into a cardioid's rear null or a supercardioid's nulls near 126°. EQ notches at ringing frequencies only buy a few dB, because the next peak in the loop response takes over.

Real rooms are not free fields. Beyond the critical distance, the reverberant field dominates, and moving the speaker even farther from the mic stops helping. That is why lecterns in reverberant churches are hard, and why an automixer that keeps NOM low, plus a headset or lavalier close to the mouth, usually beats any amount of EQ.
inPractice: At your next speech or theatre job, measure Ds, D1, D2 and D0 roughly with a laser meter and calculate PAG before soundcheck. Then compare the gain you can actually reach before ringing with the estimate, and note how much each change (closer mic, fewer open mics, moving a wedge) bought you.
keyPoints: Feedback: loop gain ≥ 0 dB at a frequency where the loop phase is a whole number of cycles.
PAG = 20·log(D0·D1 / (Ds·D2)) − 10·log(NOM) − FSM (about 6 dB).
NAG = 20·log(D0 / EAD); the system works only if PAG ≥ NAG.
Halving talker-to-mic distance gives +6 dB; doubling open mics costs 3 dB.
Notch EQ adds only a few dB; geometry, directivity and fewer open mics add more.
Beyond critical distance, moving the speaker farther away stops helping.
mistake: Many engineers try to ring out a system with a graphic EQ until it is safe. That buys a few dB at best and makes the system sound thin; getting the mic closer to the source or closing unused mics is worth far more.
sayIt: The closer the mic is to your mouth and the fewer mics are open, the louder I can make you before it starts to howl.
summary: Feedback starts when the loop from microphone to amplifier to loudspeaker and back to the microphone has a gain of 0 dB or more at a frequency where the loop phase adds up to a whole number of cycles. Potential acoustic gain (PAG) is how much gain a system can give before that happens; needed acoustic gain (NAG) is how much it must give to be useful.

terms.def: Potential acoustic gain: the maximum gain a system can provide before feedback, after a stability margin.
Needed acoustic gain: the gain required for distant listeners to hear as if they were at the equivalent acoustic distance.
Equivalent acoustic distance: how close a listener would need to be to the unamplified talker to hear equally well.
Number of open microphones; each doubling reduces PAG by 3 dB.
Feedback stability margin, usually 6 dB, kept so the system does not ring.

title: Gain before feedback: PAG and NAG

body:
Wavelength is the speed of sound divided by frequency: λ = c / f, with c about 343 m/s at 20 °C. So 100 Hz has a wavelength of 3.43 m, 1 kHz about 34 cm and 10 kHz about 3.4 cm. When sound meets an object, compare the object to that number. If the object is much smaller than the wavelength, the wave flows round it as if it were not there. If it is much larger, the high frequencies are blocked and a shadow forms behind it, while lower frequencies still bend in at the edges.

This is why a gobo or acoustic screen works on cymbals but not on kick drum or bass amp. A 1.2 m panel is several wavelengths wide at 2 kHz but only a third of a wavelength at 100 Hz. It is also why you hear the bass of a festival over a hill long after the vocals have gone. Outdoor noise barriers are judged by the extra path length δ that sound must travel over the top. The Fresnel number N = 2δ / λ grows with frequency, and Maekawa's chart (approximated by A ≈ 10·log10(3 + 20N) dB) shows attenuation rising from a few dB at low N to around 20 dB in practice. Low frequencies, with small N, get the least.

The same idea shapes loudspeakers and microphones. A speaker's front baffle is large compared with high-frequency wavelengths, so it radiates them forwards into half-space, but at low frequencies sound wraps round the cabinet into full space. That baffle step costs up to about 6 dB on axis, with a transition near f ≈ 115 / W, where W is the baffle width in metres. Microphones follow the same rule in reverse: a body or diaphragm comparable to the wavelength shadows sound arriving from the side or rear, so pressure omnis become directional at high frequencies, and large-diaphragm mics more so.

Your own head is a diffracting object about 17–18 cm wide. Below roughly 1.5 kHz sound bends round it and you locate sources mainly by time difference between the ears. Above that, the head shadows the far ear, and level difference takes over. Binaural and HRTF rendering is largely a model of this diffraction.
inPractice: Next time you place a gobo, solo the spill mic and sweep a low-pass and high-pass filter: you will hear the screen cutting cymbal spill while kick and bass come through almost unchanged. Use distance, mic pattern and the source's own directivity for low-frequency separation.
keyPoints: λ = c / f: 100 Hz ≈ 3.4 m, 1 kHz ≈ 34 cm, 10 kHz ≈ 3.4 cm.
Obstacles smaller than the wavelength barely matter; larger ones cast a shadow.
Screens, gobos and barriers work on highs, hardly on lows.
Barrier attenuation rises with Fresnel number N = 2δ / λ.
Baffle step: up to about 6 dB loss below f ≈ 115 / W (W in metres).
Head shadow makes level differences the main cue above about 1.5 kHz.
mistake: A common belief is that a heavier or thicker screen will stop bass spill. Mass helps with transmission through the panel, but sound goes round the edges; at low frequencies the panel is too small compared with the wavelength to cast a shadow.
sayIt: Low notes have waves several metres long, so they flow round walls, screens and people, while high notes are short enough to be blocked.
summary: Diffraction is the bending and spreading of sound around obstacles and through openings. How much a wave diffracts depends on the size of the object compared with the wavelength: objects much smaller than the wavelength barely affect it, while objects much larger cast a clear acoustic shadow.

terms.def: Bending and spreading of a wave around obstacles and through openings.
Region behind an object where higher frequencies are reduced because the object is large compared with their wavelength.
N = 2δ / λ, where δ is the extra path over a barrier; higher N means more attenuation.
The rise of up to about 6 dB on axis as a speaker moves from radiating into full space at low frequencies to half-space at high frequencies.
Level reduction at the far ear caused by the head blocking higher frequencies.

title: Diffraction: why bass ignores obstacles

body:
Picture a mixer and an amplifier, each plugged into a different mains socket, joined by an audio cable. The safety earths of the two sockets are connected back at the distribution board, and the cable shield connects the two chassis again. That closed loop behaves like a one-turn transformer winding: mains wiring nearby induces current in it, and small leakage currents from power supplies add more. In Italy the result is a 50 Hz hum. If the current has sharp edges, from rectifiers or switch-mode supplies, it becomes a buzz with strong harmonics at 100, 150, 200 Hz and up.

Whether you hear it depends on the interface. In an unbalanced cable the shield is also the signal return, so any current in it drops a voltage that adds straight to the signal. Ohm's law gives the size: 20 mA through a shield of 0.05 Ω is 1 mV. Against a −10 dBV consumer line level (about 316 mV) that is only 50 dB down, which is clearly audible in quiet passages. A balanced input instead measures the difference between two conductors. Noise that appears equally on both is common-mode and is rejected by the input's common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR): 60 dB of CMRR turns 100 mV of common-mode noise into 0.1 mV.

Balanced lines only work if the equipment is built properly. Neil Muncy's 'pin 1 problem' describes devices that connect the cable shield to the circuit-board ground rather than directly to the chassis where the cable enters. Shield current then flows through the audio ground inside the device and appears as hum even on a balanced line. AES48 sets out the correct practice: shield to chassis at the point of entry.

The fixes, in order: power all connected audio gear from the same distribution point to keep the loop small; use balanced connections; use an isolation transformer or a DI with a ground lift, which breaks the shield connection at one end while leaving the signal path intact; and keep audio cables away from mains and dimmer runs. Never remove or lift the mains safety earth. It is what protects people if a device develops a fault, and a stage full of metal and wet hands is where that matters most.
inPractice: When hum appears, disconnect cables one at a time from the destination back towards the sources until it stops, to find the loop. Then try the ground-lift switch on a DI or an isolation transformer on that one link, and check that every device is powered from the same distribution point.
keyPoints: A ground loop needs two earth paths between devices: the cable shield plus mains earth, or two cable shields.
Hum is 50 Hz in Italy; buzz adds harmonics at 100, 150, 200 Hz and up.
In unbalanced cables shield current becomes signal: V = I × R adds straight to the audio.
Balanced inputs reject common-mode noise by their CMRR; 60 dB means a factor of 1,000.
The 'pin 1 problem' is a design fault: the shield must go to chassis, not to circuit ground.
Fix with a shared power point, balanced lines, isolation transformers or a DI ground lift; never lift mains earth.
mistake: Many people 'fix' hum by cutting off or taping over the mains earth pin. That can leave chassis and mic bodies live if a fault occurs; the correct fix is to break the loop in the signal path with a transformer or ground lift.
sayIt: The hum is current going round a loop made by two earth connections between your gear, and we fix it by breaking that loop in the audio path, never by removing the safety earth.
summary: A ground loop forms when two pieces of equipment are connected both through a signal cable's shield and through separate earth paths, such as their mains plugs. Stray magnetic fields and leakage currents drive current around that loop, and wherever the current flows through a conductor that is also part of the audio path, its voltage drop is heard as hum or buzz.

terms.def: A closed conductive path formed by two or more earth connections between devices, in which induced current flows.
Noise that appears equally on both conductors of a balanced line, relative to ground.
Common-mode rejection ratio: how strongly a balanced input attenuates common-mode noise, in dB.
A design fault where the cable shield is tied to internal audio ground instead of the chassis, so shield current causes hum.
A switch, usually on a DI box, that disconnects the cable shield from ground at one end to break a loop.
A transformer that passes the audio signal magnetically while providing no direct electrical connection between the two sides.

title: Ground loops: where hum comes from and how to kill it safely

body:
A first-order filter rolls off at 6 dB per octave, which is the same as 20 dB per decade. Each extra order adds another 6 dB per octave, so a second-order filter falls at 12 dB per octave and a fourth-order at 24 dB per octave. The quoted cutoff of a Butterworth high-pass or low-pass is its −3 dB point, and the slope only settles to its full rate about an octave beyond it. A second-order Butterworth high-pass at 100 Hz is about −3 dB at 100 Hz and about −12 dB at 50 Hz. A second-order filter with Q above 0.707 starts to bump up just before the cutoff, which is why some high-pass filters have a 'resonance' control.

For bells, Q = centre frequency ÷ bandwidth, with bandwidth measured between the −3 dB points. In octaves, a 1-octave band is Q ≈ 1.41, a 2-octave band is Q ≈ 0.67 and a 1/3-octave band is Q ≈ 4.32. Higher Q means a narrower band. Manufacturers do not all measure bandwidth the same way on boost and cut, so the same Q number can sound different between two EQs.

Ordinary analogue-style EQs are minimum-phase: changing the level also shifts the phase near the band. A first-order high-pass has 45° of phase shift at its cutoff, a second-order Butterworth 90°, and a fourth-order 180°. Steeper filters also add more group delay around the cutoff, which can soften the attack of a kick or bass if you set a steep high-pass close to the fundamental. Linear-phase EQs avoid phase shift but add latency and can cause pre-ringing before transients.

In practice: on dialogue, a 12 or 18 dB per octave high-pass around 80–100 Hz removes rumble without thinning most voices; on a mix bus, a gentle 6 dB per octave or a shelf is safer. For crossovers and sub splits, Linkwitz-Riley filters are used because each side is −6 dB at the crossover and the two outputs sum flat. For corrective cuts, use a narrow Q to remove a resonance without taking the surrounding tone; for tonal shaping, use a wide Q and small gain changes.
inPractice: On a dialogue track, sweep a high-pass from 40 Hz upwards at 12 dB per octave and then at 24 dB per octave, and note where each one starts to thin the voice. Then solo a narrow bell at Q 8 with a big boost, find a resonance, and cut it by only 3–4 dB.
keyPoints: Each filter order adds 6 dB per octave (20 dB per decade).
A Butterworth cutoff is the −3 dB point; full slope arrives about an octave later.
Q = centre frequency ÷ bandwidth; 1 octave ≈ Q 1.41, 1/3 octave ≈ Q 4.32.
Minimum-phase filters shift phase: 45° at cutoff for first order, 90° for second, 180° for fourth.
Linkwitz-Riley crossovers are −6 dB per side at the crossover and sum flat.
Narrow Q for surgical cuts, wide Q and small gain for tone.
mistake: Many people think the cutoff frequency is where a filter 'stops' the sound. At the cutoff a Butterworth filter has only taken off 3 dB; meaningful attenuation starts an octave or more beyond it.
sayIt: The slope says how fast the filter fades out the frequencies you don't want, and the Q says how wide a slice of the spectrum a boost or cut touches.
summary: Every EQ band is a filter defined by its type, frequency, gain and either slope (for high- and low-pass filters) or Q (for bells and some shelves). Slope comes from filter order: each order adds 6 dB per octave. Q describes how narrow a band is: centre frequency divided by bandwidth.

terms.def: The number of reactive stages or poles in a filter; each adds 6 dB per octave of slope.
Quality factor: centre frequency divided by the −3 dB bandwidth. Higher Q means a narrower band.
A filter design with the flattest possible passband and a −3 dB cutoff point.
Two cascaded Butterworth filters, −6 dB at the crossover, whose low and high outputs sum flat.
How much a filter delays different frequencies; it rises near the cutoff of steep minimum-phase filters.
A filter that boosts or cuts everything above or below a frequency by a set amount.

title: Filter slopes and Q: what an EQ band really does

body:
Each bit of linear PCM doubles the number of amplitude steps, which is worth about 6.02 dB. For a full-scale sine wave, the theoretical signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio is 6.02·N + 1.76 dB: about 98 dB for 16-bit and 146 dB for 24-bit. Real converters stop well short of the 24-bit figure; the best are around 120–130 dB, limited by analogue noise, so the bottom bits of a 24-bit recording hold the converter's own noise. Bit depth sets the noise floor, not the 'resolution' of loud signals: a 16-bit file peaking at −30 dBFS uses only about 11 bits' worth of range above its floor.

Without dither, quantisation error follows the signal. On quiet material such as reverb tails and fades it becomes audible distortion that is correlated with the music. Adding dither, usually TPDF (triangular) noise of about ±1 LSB, makes the error random and independent of the signal, so you hear a steady, faint hiss instead of grit. The cost is a noise floor about 4.77 dB higher than the theoretical undithered figure. Noise-shaped dither moves much of that noise to high frequencies where the ear is less sensitive, so it sounds quieter even though its total power is higher.

32-bit float uses a 24-bit mantissa and an 8-bit exponent. Precision stays roughly 24-bit at any level, and the range runs to well over 1,000 dB, so a signal pushed over 0 dBFS inside a DAW is not clipped and can be brought back down later. That safety ends at any fixed-point stage: a converter, a 24-bit file or a plugin that clips internally. 32-bit float field recorders get their range from two converters at different gains blended together, not from a single converter with 32 bits of real dynamic range.

In practice: record at 24-bit (or 32-bit float where the recorder supports it), keep the session in float, and dither once, at the final reduction to a fixed bit depth, usually 16-bit for CD-style masters. Do not dither repeatedly at every bounce, and do not normalise or change gain after dithering. When delivering 24-bit, dither is technically correct but its effect sits below the converter noise.
inPractice: Take a reverb tail, lower it by 40 dB, and bounce it to 16-bit with dither off and then on. Raise both by 40 dB and listen: the undithered version crackles and distorts as it fades, the dithered one fades into smooth hiss.
keyPoints: Each bit is worth about 6 dB; 16-bit ≈ 98 dB, 24-bit ≈ 146 dB in theory.
Real converters reach about 120–130 dB, so analogue noise fills the lowest 24-bit steps.
Dither turns correlated quantisation distortion into steady noise.
TPDF dither raises the noise floor by about 4.77 dB; noise shaping makes it sound quieter.
32-bit float has huge headroom inside the DAW, but any fixed-point stage still clips at 0 dBFS.
Dither once, at the last reduction in bit depth, and change nothing after it.
mistake: Many people think 32-bit float recorders capture 1,500 dB of dynamic range. The file format can hold it, but the recording is still limited by the mic, the preamp and the converters, which together stay well below 150 dB.
sayIt: Bit depth decides how quiet the background hiss can be, and dither is a tiny, controlled hiss we add at the very end so quiet fades stay smooth instead of gritty.
summary: Bit depth sets how finely each sample's amplitude is measured, and so the level of the quantisation noise floor. Dither is a small, deliberate noise added before reducing bit depth so that the error becomes benign noise instead of distortion. 32-bit float stores samples as a mantissa and exponent, giving enormous headroom inside the computer, but it does not make a converter quieter.

terms.def: Least significant bit: the smallest amplitude step a given bit depth can represent.
Triangular-probability noise of about ±1 LSB that makes quantisation error independent of the signal.
Filtering the dither and requantisation noise so more of it falls where hearing is less sensitive.
The part of a floating-point number that holds its significant digits; 24 bits of precision in 32-bit float.
Simply dropping the lower bits when reducing bit depth, which leaves signal-correlated distortion.

title: Bit depth, dither and 32-bit float
Subtractive synthesis: oscillator, filter, amplifier
summary: Subtractive synthesis starts with a harmonically rich waveform and removes parts of its spectrum with a filter, then shapes level over time with an amplifier controlled by an envelope. Almost every analogue-style synth, and many sound-design patches, follow this oscillator–filter–amplifier chain.
body:
The oscillator supplies the raw spectrum, and each basic waveform has a fixed harmonic recipe. A sawtooth contains every harmonic, with the nth harmonic at 1/n of the fundamental's amplitude, so the 2nd is about 6 dB down and the 3rd about 9.5 dB down. A square wave contains only odd harmonics, also falling at 1/n. A triangle also has only odd harmonics but they fall at 1/n², so it sounds close to a sine. A pulse wave's content depends on its duty cycle: at 25%, every 4th harmonic is missing. Noise has no pitch at all and is the usual starting point for wind, surf, snares and breaths.

The filter removes what you do not want. A low-pass filter's slope is set by its number of poles: about 6 dB per octave per pole, so 12 dB/oct for a two-pole and 24 dB/oct for a four-pole design such as the Moog ladder. Well above the cutoff, a 24 dB/oct filter attenuates a component two octaves up by roughly 48 dB. Resonance feeds part of the output back to boost a narrow band at the cutoff; at high settings many filters self-oscillate and become a sine source. Key tracking moves the cutoff with the note played: at 100%, an octave up on the keyboard doubles the cutoff frequency, so the tone stays consistent across the range.

The amplifier sets level, and envelopes make sounds move. An ADSR has three times (attack, decay, release) and one level (sustain). Routing a second envelope to the filter cutoff gives the classic pluck, where brightness falls faster than loudness, which is how most real struck and plucked sounds behave. LFOs add slow periodic change, such as vibrato on pitch or tremolo on level.

In practice, subtractive patches are the backbone of sound design for picture: risers are a filter sweep on noise or detuned saws, drones are slow filter and LFO movement, and UI sounds are short filter-enveloped blips. Understanding the waveform recipes also explains mixing behaviour: a saw bass carries strong upper harmonics that cut through on small speakers, while a triangle bass all but disappears on them.
keyPoints: Sawtooth: all harmonics at 1/n. Square: odd harmonics at 1/n. Triangle: odd harmonics at 1/n².
A filter's slope is about 6 dB per octave per pole: 12 dB/oct two-pole, 24 dB/oct four-pole.
Resonance boosts a narrow band at the cutoff; turned up far enough, many filters self-oscillate.
ADSR has three times and one level: sustain.
A separate filter envelope makes brightness change faster than loudness, the basis of plucks.
100% key tracking doubles the cutoff for each octave up the keyboard.
sayIt: We start with a buzzy, rich tone and sculpt it by filtering away what we don't need, then shape how it starts and fades.
inPractice: Load a single saw into a low-pass filter with the cutoff at minimum, then raise only the filter envelope amount with a short decay and zero sustain. Compare it with the same envelope on the amplifier alone, and listen to how the filter version reads as 'plucked' while the amplifier version just sounds short.
mistake: Many people think resonance makes a filter steeper. It does not change the slope far above the cutoff; it adds a peak at the cutoff, which also thins the passband on many designs.

terms.def: One first-order section of a filter, each adding about 6 dB per octave of slope.
Making a parameter, usually filter cutoff, follow the note played.
When filter resonance is high enough that the filter produces its own sine tone at the cutoff.
The fraction of each cycle a pulse wave spends high; 50% is a square wave.
Attack, decay, sustain, release: the four stages of a standard envelope.

title: Inverse square law and critical distance
summary: In a free field, sound from a point source spreads over a sphere, so its intensity falls with the square of distance and its level drops by about 6 dB for every doubling of distance. In a real room the reflected, reverberant sound stays roughly constant, and the critical distance is where the direct and reverberant levels are equal.
body:
A small source radiating into free space spreads its power over a sphere whose area is 4πr². Double the distance and the same power covers four times the area, so intensity falls to a quarter. That is the inverse square law: intensity is proportional to 1/r². In decibels the level change is 20·log10(r2/r1), which gives about 6 dB per doubling of distance and 20 dB per tenfold change. The law only holds in the far field, once you are several times the size of the source away, and in free-field conditions. A long line source, such as a line array heard within its near field, spreads cylindrically instead and loses only about 3 dB per doubling.

Indoors, every surface adds reflections. Close to the source the direct sound dominates and follows the inverse square law. Further away the reverberant field takes over, and its level is roughly the same throughout the room. The critical distance (dc) is the point where the two are equal. A common estimate is dc ≈ 0.057·√(Q·V/RT60), with V the room volume in m³, RT60 in seconds and Q the directivity factor of the source (1 for an omni). Larger, deader rooms and more directional sources push dc further out. Because dc depends on the square root, halving RT60 only increases it by about 1.4 times.

For recording, the critical distance tells you how much room you will capture. Inside dc the mic hears mostly direct sound; outside it, mostly room. A directional mic raises the effective distance at which it gives the same direct-to-reverberant ratio, which is why a cardioid can sit further back than an omni for a similar sound. On location, keeping the boom well inside dc keeps dialogue clear in a reflective set.

In live sound and monitoring the same idea applies. Listeners far beyond dc hear mostly the room, so more level does not buy more clarity. A more directional loudspeaker, aimed at the audience and away from walls, extends the distance over which direct sound dominates. In the studio, a listening position well inside dc of the monitors keeps the stereo image stable.
keyPoints: Point source in free field: −6 dB per doubling of distance.
Level change = 20·log10(r2/r1); ×10 distance = −20 dB.
Line source in its near field: about −3 dB per doubling.
Critical distance: direct level equals reverberant level.
dc ≈ 0.057·√(Q·V/RT60); grows with directivity and absorption.
Beyond dc, moving further away barely changes the total level.
sayIt: Close to the source you hear the instrument; past a certain point in this room you mostly hear the room, so moving the mic changes the balance a lot.
inPractice: Walk a handheld SPL meter away from a speaker playing pink noise in a live room and note where the level stops falling by 6 dB per doubling. That is roughly your critical distance; place your close mics well inside it and your room mics outside it.
mistake: Many people expect the inverse square law to hold everywhere indoors. It only describes the direct sound; past the critical distance the reverberant field dominates and the level stays roughly constant.

terms.def: Intensity from a point source in a free field falls in proportion to 1/r².
A space with no reflections, such as an anechoic chamber or open air well away from surfaces.
The distance from a source at which direct and reverberant sound levels are equal.
The ratio of on-axis intensity of a source to that of an omni source radiating the same total power.
The diffuse sound built up from many reflections, roughly uniform in level through a room.

title: Room modes and RT60
summary: Room modes are standing waves that form between surfaces at frequencies set by the room's dimensions, giving uneven bass from seat to seat. RT60 is the time sound takes to decay by 60 dB after the source stops, and Sabine's formula estimates it from room volume and total absorption.
body:
Between two parallel walls a distance L apart, sound reinforces itself whenever a whole number of half-wavelengths fits between them. These axial modes fall at f = n·c/2L, where c is the speed of sound (about 343 m/s) and n = 1, 2, 3 and so on. A 5.72 m room has its first length mode near 30 Hz, then 60, 90, 120 Hz. Tangential modes involve four surfaces and oblique modes all six. They are generally weaker; axial modes are usually the strongest and cause the most trouble. Every rectangular room has modes along length, width and height, and their spacing determines how even the low end sounds.

Each mode has pressure peaks and nulls in fixed places. All modes have a pressure maximum at the walls and in the corners, which is why bass traps work best there. The first axial mode has a null halfway between its two walls, so a seat in the exact middle of the room hears that frequency weakly. As frequency rises, modes become more numerous and overlap until the room behaves statistically. The Schroeder frequency, roughly 2000·√(RT60/V), marks that transition. Below it, think in modes; above it, think in reflections and reverberation time.

RT60 is the time for sound to fall 60 dB after the source stops. Sabine's formula estimates it as RT60 = 0.161·V/A, where V is the volume in m³ and A is total absorption in metric sabins (m²), the sum of each surface area multiplied by its absorption coefficient. Double the absorption and RT60 halves. Sabine works best in fairly live rooms; in very absorbent rooms the Eyring formula is more accurate. Since absorption coefficients vary with frequency, RT60 is quoted per octave band.

In practice, a vocal booth or control room with modes that pile up near the same frequency gives a boomy note on certain bass pitches and a thin one on others. On location you hear the same thing in small rooms: some dialogue gets boomy. Move the listening position or mic off the room's centre lines, treat corners with thick absorption, and check RT60 per band so the low end is not much longer than the mids.
keyPoints: Axial modes: f = n·c/2L; strongest of the three mode types.
All modes peak at boundaries and corners.
The first axial mode has a null at the room's centre line.
Schroeder frequency ≈ 2000·√(RT60/V) separates modal and statistical behaviour.
Sabine: RT60 = 0.161·V/A; doubling absorption halves RT60.
RT60 varies with frequency, so measure it per octave band.
sayIt: This room boosts some bass notes and swallows others because of its shape, so we'll adjust where we sit and treat the corners before we touch the EQ.
inPractice: Calculate the first three axial modes for each dimension of your control room and play sine sweeps through that range. Walk the room and note where each one peaks and dips, then pick a mix position away from the nulls.
mistake: A common belief is that EQ can fix room modes for every seat. Modes change from place to place, so EQ that flattens one position can make others worse; position and treatment come first.

terms.def: A resonance of the room at which sound reflecting between surfaces forms a standing wave.
A mode between one pair of parallel surfaces, f = n·c/2L.
Time for sound to decay by 60 dB after the source stops.
Unit of absorption equal to one square metre of perfectly absorbing surface.
Approximate frequency above which modes overlap densely enough for the room to behave statistically.

title: Masking and equal-loudness contours
summary: Masking is when one sound makes another harder or impossible to hear, either at the same time or just before or after it. Equal-loudness contours show the sound pressure level needed at each frequency to sound as loud as a 1 kHz reference, and they change shape with level.
body:
The ear analyses sound in overlapping frequency bands called critical bands. A loud sound raises the threshold of hearing for quieter sounds near its frequency; that is simultaneous masking. Masking spreads further upward in frequency than downward, especially at high levels. One common measure of auditory filter width is the equivalent rectangular bandwidth (ERB), which Glasberg and Moore estimate as 24.7·(4.37·f/1000 + 1) Hz, about 130 Hz at 1 kHz. Two sounds inside the same band compete hard; sounds further apart in frequency compete much less.

Masking also works in time. A loud sound hides quieter sounds that follow it for a while; this forward masking can last around 100 to 200 ms. Backward masking, where a later loud sound hides an earlier quiet one, is much shorter, typically a few milliseconds up to roughly 20 ms. Perceptual codecs such as MP3 and AAC rely on both kinds of masking to decide which parts of a signal can be coded with less precision.

Equal-loudness contours, first measured by Fletcher and Munson and now standardised in ISO 226, plot the SPL needed at each frequency for a pure tone to sound as loud as a 1 kHz tone. The unit of loudness level is the phon: a sound at N phon is as loud as a 1 kHz tone at N dB SPL. The ear is most sensitive around 2 to 5 kHz and much less sensitive in the low bass. At low levels the contours rise steeply at low frequencies, and they bunch closer together there, so bass loudness grows faster than midrange loudness as you turn up. Perceived loudness in sones doubles for about every 10 phon increase above 40 phon, where 40 phon is 1 sone.

In a mix, masking explains why a bass and kick that both sit around the same low frequencies blur together, and why dialogue gets buried under music or effects sharing its 1 to 4 kHz range. Cutting space in one track often works better than boosting another. Equal-loudness contours explain why mixes balanced quietly sound bass-heavy when played loud, so check at a calibrated reference level, such as the level your delivery standard or room calls for.
keyPoints: Simultaneous masking is strongest within a critical band.
Masking spreads more upward in frequency than downward.
Forward masking lasts much longer than backward masking.
Phon: loudness level equal to the dB SPL of an equally loud 1 kHz tone.
40 phon = 1 sone; +10 phon roughly doubles loudness.
Contours bunch at low frequencies, so bass gets louder faster as level rises.
sayIt: The guitar is hiding the vocal because they live in the same frequency range, so I'm carving a little space rather than just turning the vocal up.
inPractice: On your next dialogue mix, solo the music and find where it sits in the 1 to 4 kHz range. Dip it a few dB there only while dialogue plays and compare intelligibility against simply lowering the music.
mistake: People often fix a masked sound by boosting it. Reducing the competing sound in the shared band usually restores clarity with less level build-up and less harshness.

terms.def: A sound becoming inaudible because another sound near its frequency is present at the same time.
A loud sound raising the threshold for quiet sounds that follow it in time.
The frequency range over which the ear integrates energy; sounds within it mask each other strongly.
Unit of loudness level, equal to the SPL of a 1 kHz tone judged equally loud.
Unit of perceived loudness; 1 sone is the loudness of a 40 phon sound.

title: Localisation: ITD, ILD and HRTF
summary: We locate sounds mainly through the interaural time difference (ITD) and interaural level difference (ILD) between our two ears, plus the direction-dependent filtering of the head, torso and outer ear described by the head-related transfer function (HRTF). Each cue works best in a different frequency range.
body:
A sound from one side reaches the near ear first. That interaural time difference is zero straight ahead and reaches roughly 0.6 to 0.7 ms for a source at 90°. Woodworth's model estimates it as ITD = (r/c)·(θ + sin θ), with r the head radius (about 8.75 cm) and θ in radians. At low frequencies, below about 1.5 kHz, the ear compares the phase of the waveform at each ear. Above that, a wavelength is short compared with the head and phase becomes ambiguous, so timing comes mainly from the envelope of the sound.

The head also blocks sound. At high frequencies the far ear sits in an acoustic shadow, creating an interaural level difference that can exceed 20 dB at some angles and frequencies. Low frequencies diffract around the head, so ILD is small there. This split, timing at low frequencies and level at high frequencies, is Rayleigh's duplex theory.

ITD and ILD alone cannot tell front from back or up from down. Every point on a 'cone of confusion' around the axis through the ears gives the same pair of values. The HRTF resolves this. The folds of the pinna, plus reflections from the shoulders and torso, add direction-dependent peaks and notches, mostly above about 5 kHz. The brain learns these patterns for your own ears. Small head movements also help: turning the head changes ITD and ILD in opposite ways for a source in front and one behind.

These cues explain much of everyday practice. Spaced microphone pairs record time differences; coincident pairs record level differences. Pan pots create level differences between speakers, and the listener's ears turn those into usable cues. Binaural recording with a dummy head captures ITD, ILD and a generic HRTF, which works on headphones but loses its effect on speakers, where each ear hears both channels. Immersive mixing for headphones uses HRTF rendering, and results vary between listeners because their ears differ from the model. On set, a lavalier mic sitting on the chest misses the head and pinna filtering altogether, which is part of why it sounds different from a boom.
keyPoints: ITD: up to about 0.6 to 0.7 ms at 90°; dominant below about 1.5 kHz.
ILD: from head shadowing; significant at high frequencies.
Duplex theory: time cues low, level cues high.
Cone of confusion: ITD and ILD alone cannot separate front, back and elevation.
HRTF: pinna, head and torso filtering, mostly above about 5 kHz.
Head movement resolves front/back ambiguity.
sayIt: Your ears place sounds using tiny timing and level differences plus the way your outer ear colours sound, so headphone surround never sounds exactly the same for everyone.
inPractice: Record the same source with a spaced omni pair and a coincident XY pair, then listen on speakers and headphones. Note how timing differences give width and spaciousness, while level differences give a sharper, more stable image.
mistake: Many assume binaural recordings work equally well on loudspeakers. On speakers each ear hears both channels, which scrambles the interaural cues unless crosstalk cancellation is used.

terms.def: Interaural time difference: the difference in arrival time of a sound at the two ears.
Interaural level difference: the difference in level at the two ears, caused mainly by head shadowing.
Head-related transfer function: the direction-dependent filtering of sound by the head, torso and pinnae.
The set of source positions that produce the same ITD and ILD.
Rayleigh's model that ITD governs low-frequency and ILD high-frequency lateral localisation.

title: Balanced and unbalanced lines, and DI boxes
summary: A balanced line carries signal on two conductors with equal impedances to ground, plus a separate shield, so interference that hits both conductors equally is rejected at a differential input. An unbalanced line uses one conductor and the shield as the return. A DI box converts a high-impedance unbalanced source into a low-impedance balanced signal for a mic input.
body:
In an unbalanced connection the shield carries both the signal return and any interference or ground current. Any voltage dropped along the shield adds directly to the signal. That is why unbalanced lines are kept short and are prone to hum. A balanced connection has two signal conductors, hot (pin 2) and cold (pin 3), plus a shield (pin 1). The receiving input amplifies only the difference between hot and cold. Noise picked up equally on both conductors, called common-mode noise, cancels. How well it cancels is the common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR), quoted in dB.

What makes a line balanced is equal impedance from each conductor to ground, not equal and opposite signals. An impedance-balanced output drives signal on pin 2 only and ties pin 3 to ground through a resistor matching pin 2's output impedance. It still rejects interference perfectly well. Symmetrical signals simply add headroom. Transformer-balanced inputs and outputs give galvanic isolation as well, which can break ground loops.

A DI (direct injection) box solves a different problem. Guitars, basses and many keyboards have high source impedances and unbalanced outputs. Long cables add capacitance that, with a high source impedance, forms a low-pass filter: 20 kΩ driving 1.5 nF of cable gives a corner around 5 kHz. A DI presents a high input impedance to the instrument and delivers a low-impedance balanced signal at roughly mic level. A passive DI uses a step-down transformer: a 12:1 turns ratio drops voltage by about 21.6 dB and reflects the load impedance up by 144 times. An active DI uses an amplifier, usually powered by phantom power or a battery, and typically offers an input impedance around 1 MΩ.

On stage, a DI lets you run a bass or keyboard down a long multicore with mic channels. In the studio it gives a clean DI track alongside the amp mic for reamping. Most DIs also have a ground-lift switch and a thru jack to feed the amp. In post and field work, DIs and line-to-mic transformers isolate a client's laptop or a venue feed from your recorder and cut hum.
keyPoints: Balanced = equal impedances to ground on hot and cold.
The differential input rejects common-mode noise; CMRR measures how well.
Impedance-balanced outputs are still balanced connections.
Unbalanced lines carry signal return on the shield, so they pick up hum.
Passive DI: step-down transformer; active DI: powered, high input impedance.
A transformer's impedance ratio is the square of its turns ratio.
sayIt: I'm running your keyboard through a DI so it can travel the length of the stage without picking up hum or losing top end.
inPractice: Plug a passive bass into a line input through 10 m of instrument cable, then through a DI at the bass with a long mic cable to the desk. Compare top end and hum; then try the DI's ground lift if there is any buzz.
mistake: Many believe balanced means two opposite-polarity copies of the signal. Rejection depends on matched impedances to ground; a line with signal on only one leg can still be fully balanced.

terms.def: Two signal conductors with equal impedances to ground, received by a differential input.
Interference that appears equally on both conductors of a balanced line.
Common-mode rejection ratio: how strongly an input rejects common-mode signals, in dB.
An output driving one leg while the other has matching impedance to ground but no signal.
A device converting a high-impedance unbalanced source to a low-impedance balanced output.
A switch that breaks the shield connection between input and output grounds to stop ground-loop hum.

title: dB scales: dBu, dBV, dBFS and dB SPL
