summary: A decibel is a logarithmic ratio, so every dB scale needs a stated reference. dBu is referenced to 0.775 V, dBV to 1 V, dBFS to digital full scale and dB SPL to 20 µPa of sound pressure.
body:
The decibel expresses a ratio on a logarithmic scale. For power quantities it is 10·log10(P1/P0). For field quantities such as voltage and sound pressure it is 20·log10(V1/V0), because power is proportional to the square of voltage or pressure. Doubling voltage is +6 dB; doubling power is +3 dB. Ten times the power is +10 dB; ten times the voltage is +20 dB. A bare 'dB' is only a difference. Adding a suffix fixes the reference and turns it into an absolute level.

dBu is referenced to 0.775 V RMS, the voltage that delivers 1 mW into 600 Ω. Professional line level is +4 dBu, about 1.23 V. dBV is referenced to 1 V RMS. Consumer line level is −10 dBV, about 0.316 V. The two scales differ by a fixed 2.2 dB: 0 dBV = +2.2 dBu. So the gap between +4 dBu and −10 dBV is about 11.8 dB, not 14 dB. The older dBm refers to 1 mW of power and only matches dBu when the load is 600 Ω.

dBFS is referenced to digital full scale, the largest value a fixed-point converter can code. Levels in dBFS are zero or negative, and nothing above 0 dBFS can be stored in fixed point. The analogue voltage that matches 0 dBFS depends on the converter's alignment; common studio and broadcast alignments put it anywhere from around +18 to +24 dBu. dB SPL measures sound pressure against 20 µPa, the nominal threshold of hearing at 1 kHz. 1 Pa is about 94 dB SPL, which is why calibrators use 94 dB and 114 dB.

In practice you move between these scales all the time. A mic turns dB SPL into a voltage in dBV. A preamp adds gain in dB and outputs dBu. A converter maps dBu to dBFS. On location, matching a mixer's output to a camera input means knowing whether each end works at mic level, −10 dBV or +4 dBu. On a PA, amplifier power follows the 10·log rule, so ten times the power gives only 10 dB more level.
keyPoints: Power: 10·log10. Voltage and pressure: 20·log10.
0 dBu = 0.775 V; 0 dBV = 1 V; 0 dBV ≈ +2.2 dBu.
0 dBFS is the fixed-point ceiling; its analogue level depends on alignment.
0 dB SPL = 20 µPa; 1 Pa ≈ 94 dB SPL.
A bare dB is a ratio; a suffix makes it an absolute level.
sayIt: That number is a level relative to a reference, so +4 on the console and −10 on the camera are not the same thing; I'll match them so nothing distorts.
inPractice: Send a 1 kHz tone at a known dBFS from your recorder and measure the output voltage with a true-RMS meter. Convert it to dBu and dBV and write down your device's alignment for the next job.
mistake: People often treat +4 dBu and −10 dBV as 14 dB apart. Because the references differ by 2.2 dB, the real gap is about 11.8 dB.

terms.def: Voltage level referenced to 0.775 V RMS.
Voltage level referenced to 1 V RMS.
Digital level referenced to the full-scale maximum of a fixed-point system.
Sound pressure level referenced to 20 µPa.
The agreed relationship between an analogue level and a digital level, such as a reference tone in dBFS.

title: Linear-phase vs minimum-phase EQ
summary: A minimum-phase EQ, like any analogue EQ, shifts phase wherever it changes gain, but adds no latency and puts all of its ringing after the input. A linear-phase EQ delays every frequency by the same amount, so it adds no phase distortion, at the cost of latency and ringing that starts before the sound it is filtering (pre-ringing).
body:
Every analogue EQ and most digital ones are minimum-phase. In a minimum-phase filter, the phase response is fixed by the magnitude response: wherever the gain changes, the phase shifts, and where the response is flat, it does not. Different frequencies come out with slightly different delays. The output never comes before the input, so the only ringing is after the event. The filter adds no latency beyond the system's normal buffer, which is why it is the right choice for tracking, live mixing and monitoring.

A linear-phase EQ is built as a finite impulse response (FIR) filter with a symmetric impulse response. Every frequency is delayed by the same time, so the waveform shape is kept and only the tone changes. A symmetric FIR of N taps delays everything by (N − 1)/2 samples. That delay is the plugin's latency. A filter reporting 3072 samples of latency at 48 kHz is 64 ms late. The DAW's delay compensation hides this on playback, but it makes the plugin useless for live monitoring.

The symmetric impulse response also means that any ringing appears equally before and after the main peak. This is pre-ringing. It grows with the narrowness, depth and steepness of the EQ move and with lower frequencies, because those filters need longer impulse responses. A steep linear-phase high-pass or a narrow low-frequency cut on a kick or snare can produce an audible swell or 'suck' before each hit. Ears are much less forgiving of energy before a transient than after it, because post-ringing is masked by the transient itself.

Choose by the job. Use linear-phase when you EQ one of several correlated signals and must not change their phase relationship. Examples are a snare top mic against its bottom mic, the mid or side of an M/S signal, a band in a multiband split, or parallel paths that will be summed again. In mastering it is also used for gentle broad moves. Use minimum-phase for steep or narrow corrective moves on transient material, for anything live, and whenever latency matters. On dialogue, a minimum-phase high-pass is usually the cleaner choice, because pre-ringing on plosives and footsteps is easy to hear.
keyPoints: Minimum-phase: phase shift only where the gain changes, no latency, ringing only after the event.
Linear-phase: equal delay at all frequencies, so no phase distortion.
Symmetric FIR latency = (N − 1)/2 samples; 3072 samples at 48 kHz is 64 ms.
Pre-ringing grows with steep, narrow and low-frequency moves.
Use linear-phase on correlated or parallel signals; minimum-phase for live work and transients.
sayIt: This EQ keeps the timing of every frequency identical, but it needs a little time to work, so we use it in the mix rather than while you are recording.
inPractice: Put a steep 80 Hz high-pass on a dry snare, first in minimum-phase mode and then in linear-phase mode, and compare. Zoom in on the waveform and you will see energy appear before each hit in linear-phase mode; listen for the soft swell that comes with it.
mistake: Many people assume linear-phase EQ is always higher quality. It only removes phase shift; it adds latency and pre-ringing, and on transient material a minimum-phase EQ often sounds cleaner.

terms.def: A filter whose phase shift is fixed by its magnitude response and whose output never comes before its input. All analogue EQs are minimum-phase.
A filter that delays all frequencies by the same time, so the waveform shape is kept. In audio it is built as a symmetric FIR filter.
Filter ringing that appears before a transient. It comes from the symmetric impulse response of a linear-phase filter.
The time delay a filter gives to each frequency. It is constant for a linear-phase filter and varies with frequency for a minimum-phase one.
The DAW feature that delays other tracks by a plugin's reported latency so everything stays in time.

title: Clocking, jitter and sample-rate conversion
summary: Every digital audio device needs a sample clock, and devices that exchange digital audio must share one clock or their sample rates will drift apart. Jitter is short-term variation in the timing of that clock; it only degrades audio at the moments of conversion. Sample-rate conversion recalculates a signal at a new rate, filtering to the new Nyquist limit.
body:
When digital devices pass audio to each other, they must run at exactly the same rate. One device is the master and every other device follows it, through word clock on 75 Ω coaxial cable, through the clock embedded in an AES3 or ADAT stream, or from a video reference such as black burst or tri-level sync. If two devices each run on their own crystal, their rates differ by a few parts per million. At 48 kHz, a 20 ppm difference adds up to 1728 samples, or 36 ms, in 30 minutes. The receiver must then drop or repeat samples, and you hear periodic clicks. Daisy-chained word clock should be terminated in 75 Ω at the last device, or reflections can make the clock unreliable.

Jitter is the random or periodic wobble in the timing of each clock edge. Interface jitter on a cable only matters if it causes data errors. It does not change the samples themselves. Sampling jitter at the ADC or DAC does matter, because a sample taken or played at the wrong moment has the wrong value. For a full-scale sine, the best possible signal-to-noise ratio is SNR = −20·log10(2π·f·tj), where tj is the RMS jitter. At 1 kHz with 1 ns of jitter, that is about 104 dB. At 20 kHz it falls to about 78 dB. Good converters use a phase-locked loop (PLL) to clean up an incoming clock. Independent tests have shown that an external master clock rarely improves a good converter's internal clock, and can make it slightly worse.

Sample-rate conversion (SRC) rebuilds the signal at a new rate. When going down, it must low-pass filter below the new Nyquist frequency to stop aliasing. 96 kHz to 48 kHz is a simple 2:1 ratio. 48 kHz to 44.1 kHz is a ratio of 147/160. Synchronous SRC works between rates locked to the same clock. Asynchronous SRC (ASRC) also tracks two independent clocks, which is how many digital inputs accept an unlocked source.

In film and TV, sample rate and speed are linked. Pull-down slows audio by 0.1% (a factor of 1000/1001) to follow picture running at 23.976 or 29.97 fps. A 60-minute 48 kHz take played at 48 000/1.001 Hz lasts 60 minutes 3.6 seconds. On location, keep recorder and camera on the same project rate and frame rate, and jam timecode. In the studio, choose one clock master and check every device reports it is locked.
keyPoints: One master clock; every other device locks to it.
Unlocked devices drift: 20 ppm at 48 kHz is 36 ms in 30 minutes.
Only jitter at the ADC or DAC degrades the audio.
Jitter-limited SNR = −20·log10(2π·f·tj).
Downward SRC must filter below the new Nyquist frequency.
Pull-up and pull-down change speed by 0.1% (1000/1001).
sayIt: All the digital gear has to tick to the same clock, otherwise the audio slowly slips out of step and starts to click.
inPractice: Before the next multi-device session, draw the clock chain on paper: name the master, then check each device's lock indicator and sample-rate display. Leave a 10-minute test recording running and listen for clicks at the end before you commit to the take.
mistake: People often buy an external master clock expecting better sound from one converter. A good converter usually performs best on its own internal clock; an external clock exists to keep several devices in step.

terms.def: A square-wave clock at the sample rate, sent on 75 Ω coaxial cable, used to lock digital devices together.
Short-term variation in the timing of clock edges. It degrades audio only at the point of conversion.
Phase-locked loop: a circuit that locks a local oscillator to an incoming clock and filters out much of its jitter.
Asynchronous sample-rate converter: converts between two clocks that are not locked to each other.
Slowing audio by 0.1% (1000/1001) to match picture running at 23.976 or 29.97 fps.

title: Stereo mic techniques compared
summary: Stereo mic techniques create an image from level differences, time differences or both. Coincident pairs (XY, Blumlein, M/S) use level only and fold to mono cleanly. Spaced pairs (AB, Decca Tree) use time differences and give more spaciousness, at the cost of mono compatibility. Near-coincident pairs (ORTF) combine the two.
body:
Coincident pairs place two capsules as close together as possible, so sound reaches both at the same time. XY uses two cardioids angled between about 90° and 135°. Blumlein uses two figure-8s at 90°. It picks up the rear as strongly as the front, so the room becomes part of the sound. Sources in the side quadrants come out in opposite polarity in the two channels. Sources behind the pair appear mirrored, so rear-left is heard on the right. Because coincident pairs have no time differences, the mono sum has no comb filtering.

M/S uses a forward-facing mid mic (often a cardioid) and a sideways figure-8. You decode it as L = M + S and R = M − S, with the positive lobe of the figure-8 facing left. Raising S widens the image; muting S leaves pure mono from the mid mic. Width can be set after the recording, which is why M/S is common on location for film and TV. An M/S shotgun fits on a single boom pole, and the mid channel alone is a usable mono track.

Spaced pairs (AB) use two mics, usually omnis, from about 40 cm to a few metres apart. Time differences create the image and give a strong sense of space. Omnis also tend to have better low-frequency extension than directional mics. Summed to mono, the time differences turn into comb filtering. With 60 cm spacing, a source fully to one side arrives 1.75 ms later at the far mic, which puts the first mono notch near 286 Hz. The Decca Tree is a spaced array of three omnis. Left and right are about 2 m apart, with a centre mic forward of them. It is placed above and behind the conductor and is standard for orchestral film scoring, often with outrigger mics.

Near-coincident pairs mix the two cues. ORTF uses two cardioids 17 cm apart at 110°. The largest time difference is about 0.5 ms. NOS uses 30 cm and 90°. In practice, use XY or M/S when mono compatibility matters, as in broadcast, dialogue ambiences and overheads that may fold down. Use AB or a Decca Tree for large, natural rooms. Use ORTF as a dependable all-rounder on drums, choirs and ensembles.
keyPoints: Coincident (XY, Blumlein, M/S): level differences only, clean mono sum.
Spaced (AB, Decca): time differences, spacious, comb filtering in mono.
ORTF: cardioids 17 cm apart at 110°; NOS: 30 cm at 90°.
M/S decode: L = M + S, R = M − S; width is adjustable afterwards.
Blumlein hears the rear fully and mirrors it left to right.
Decca Tree: three omnis, standard for orchestral film scoring.
sayIt: We are using two mics arranged so the recording keeps where everything sits from left to right, and it will still sound right if someone plays it in mono.
inPractice: On your next room or ambience recording, set up an M/S pair and a 60 cm AB pair side by side. Fold both to mono and compare: the M/S pair should only lose width, while the AB pair will change in tone as well.
mistake: A common belief is that wider spacing always means a better stereo image. Too wide an AB pair leaves a 'hole in the middle', and any spacing adds comb filtering when the mix folds to mono.

terms.def: Two capsules placed at the same point, so the stereo image comes from level differences only.
Two mics, usually omnis, set apart so the stereo image comes mainly from time differences.
A near-coincident pair of cardioids 17 cm apart, angled at 110°.
Mid-side: a forward mid mic and a sideways figure-8, decoded as L = M + S and R = M − S.
Three spaced omnis, with the centre mic forward of the left and right pair, used mainly for orchestras.

title: Proximity effect and off-axis colour
summary: Proximity effect is the rise in bass response of a pressure-gradient (directional) mic when the source is close. Off-axis response is how a mic's frequency response changes away from its main axis. Both decide how close sources and spill sound, not just how loud they are.
body:
A pressure-gradient mic responds to the difference in pressure between the front and back of its diaphragm. Far from a source, that difference grows with frequency, and the mic's design corrects for it. Close to a small source, the sound waves are curved and the level falls quickly with distance. That adds an extra part to the pressure difference that does not depend on frequency. At low frequencies, this near-field part dominates, so the bass rises. A pure pressure mic (an omni) has no proximity effect.

For an ideal point source and a figure-8 mic, the bass rise compared with the far field is √(1 + 1/(kr)²), where k = 2πf/c and r is the distance. It reaches +3 dB where kr = 1, that is f = c/(2πr). At 10 cm that is about 546 Hz. A cardioid is half pressure and half gradient, so its rise is √(1 + 1/(2kr)²). It reaches +3 dB at half that frequency, about 273 Hz at 10 cm, and is about 6 dB less than a figure-8's at very low frequencies. Well below that frequency, each halving of distance adds about 6 dB of bass relative to the mids. That is on top of the general level rise.

Off-axis response is a separate effect. An ideal cardioid is 6 dB down at 90° and has its null at 180°. Real mics drift from the ideal at the extremes of the spectrum. At high frequencies, the diaphragm and body become large compared with the wavelength. A 25 mm diaphragm equals one wavelength at about 13.7 kHz, so sound from the side partly cancels across its surface and the mic becomes more directional. Off-axis sound becomes duller and often uneven. Shotgun mics are very directional at high frequencies but much less so in the bass, and their off-axis sound is clearly coloured.

This shapes daily work. A singer who 'works the mic' uses proximity effect as an EQ. A presenter who leans in sounds boomy. On a boom, keep the distance and angle consistent, because the tone of the dialogue changes with both. Lavaliers are usually omnis, partly to avoid proximity effect so close to the mouth. Spill from cymbals into a tom mic, or from the band into a vocal mic, arrives off-axis, so the tone of that spill matters as much as its level. A bass-cut switch on the mic or preamp counters proximity effect at short distances.
keyPoints: Only pressure-gradient (directional) mics show proximity effect.
Figure-8: +3 dB at f = c/(2πr); about 546 Hz at 10 cm.
Cardioid: +3 dB at half that frequency; about 6 dB less bass rise than a figure-8.
Well below the corner, halving the distance adds about 6 dB of bass.
Ideal cardioid: −6 dB at 90°, null at 180°.
Off-axis sound usually gets duller as frequency rises.
sayIt: The closer you get to this mic, the more bass it gives you, so keep a steady distance and your voice will stay the same.
inPractice: Record a talker at 5, 10, 20 and 40 cm on a cardioid, then match the levels and compare the low end. Repeat with a figure-8 ribbon and an omni, and note which mic changes most.
mistake: Some people think proximity effect is just the mic getting louder when you get closer. It is a change in tonal balance: the bass rises more than the mids, and only on directional mics.

terms.def: The rise in bass response of a pressure-gradient mic when the source is close.
A mic that responds to the pressure difference between the two sides of its diaphragm. Figure-8s are pure gradient; cardioids are partly gradient.
The region close to a source where the waves are strongly curved and level falls quickly with distance.
The change in a mic's frequency response for sound arriving away from its main axis.
A built-in high-pass filter used to counter proximity effect and low-frequency rumble.

title: Limiters, true peak, gates and expanders
summary: A limiter is a fast, high-ratio compressor that holds peaks under a ceiling. Sample-peak meters can miss the true peak of the reconstructed waveform, which can lie between samples; true-peak meters oversample to find it. Gates and downward expanders do the opposite of a compressor: they turn down signals below a threshold.
body:
A limiter is a compressor with a very high ratio, usually 10:1 or more, and a fast attack. A brickwall limiter aims for an infinite ratio, so nothing passes the ceiling. To catch fast transients without distortion, many limiters use lookahead. They delay the audio by a few milliseconds so the gain can start to fall before the peak arrives. 5 ms of lookahead at 48 kHz is 240 samples of latency. Fast release on bass-heavy material modulates the waveform and adds distortion, so good limiters use adaptive or program-dependent release.

A sample-peak meter only reads the values of the samples. The DAC rebuilds a smooth waveform that can rise above them, between samples. These are inter-sample peaks. A sine at a quarter of the sample rate, sampled 45° away from its crests, has every sample at 0.707 of the true peak. Normalised to 0 dBFS samples, its true peak is +3 dB. ITU-R BS.1770 defines true-peak measurement. It oversamples the signal, at least 4× at 48 kHz, and reports the result in dBTP. EBU R128 sets a −1 dBTP maximum, and ATSC A/85 recommends −2 dBTP. Lossy codecs can also raise peaks, so leave more headroom for streaming encodes. Use a true-peak limiter or an oversampled limiter as the last stage of a master.

A downward expander increases the dynamic range below its threshold. With a 1:2 ratio and a threshold of −40 dBFS, a −50 dBFS input comes out at −60 dBFS. A gate is an expander with a very high ratio. The range (or depth) control sets the most attenuation it can apply. Hold keeps it open for a set time after the signal drops. Hysteresis sets the close threshold lower than the open threshold, so it does not chatter on signals that hover near the threshold. A key (sidechain) filter makes the detector listen to only part of the spectrum.

In the studio, gate toms with the key filter tuned to the drum, so snare and cymbals do not open them. Use a small range rather than full muting so the kit still sounds natural. In post, a gentle expander with 6–10 dB of range lowers room tone and noise between dialogue lines with fewer audible jumps than a hard gate. Live, gates on toms and expanders on lectern mics reduce spill and help gain before feedback. For delivery, check the spec's true-peak limit and meter in dBTP, not just sample peaks.
keyPoints: Limiter: ratio 10:1 or more, fast attack; brickwall aims for ∞:1.
Lookahead removes overshoot but adds latency (5 ms = 240 samples at 48 kHz).
Inter-sample peaks can exceed sample peaks; meter in dBTP.
EBU R128: −1 dBTP max; ATSC A/85: −2 dBTP.
Expander 1:2 below threshold: every 1 dB down becomes 2 dB down.
Gate controls: threshold, range, attack, hold, release, hysteresis, key filter.
sayIt: The limiter stops the loudest moments from going over, and the gate quietly turns the mic down when nobody is playing into it.
inPractice: Take a finished master that peaks at 0 dBFS on a sample-peak meter and put a true-peak meter on it. Note how far over 0 dBTP it goes, then set a true-peak limiter to the delivery ceiling and check again after encoding to AAC.
mistake: Many engineers assume a master that peaks at 0 dBFS on a sample meter cannot clip. The reconstructed waveform can exceed 0 dBFS between samples, so a DAC or codec can clip it; measure true peak instead.

terms.def: A compressor with a very high ratio and fast attack that holds the signal under a ceiling.
A peak in the reconstructed analogue waveform that lies between samples and is higher than any sample value.
The peak level of the reconstructed waveform, measured by oversampling as defined in ITU-R BS.1770.
A processor that reduces level below a threshold by a ratio, increasing the dynamic range of quiet signals.
A gap between a gate's open and close thresholds that stops it chattering on signals near the threshold.
The maximum attenuation a gate or expander can apply.

title: Reverb and delay design
summary: Artificial reverb and delay are built from delayed copies of a signal. Pre-delay sets the gap before the reverb starts, early reflections suggest the size and shape of the space, and decay time and damping set how long the tail lasts and how its tone changes. In a delay, feedback sets how quickly the repeats die away.
body:
In a real room, the direct sound arrives first, then a set of early reflections, then a dense, decaying tail. Reverb plugins copy this structure. Pre-delay sets the gap between the direct sound and the start of the reverb. In concert-hall acoustics, the gap before the first reflection is called the initial time delay gap. Sound travels about 34 cm per millisecond, so a reflection with 6.86 m of extra path arrives 20 ms after the direct sound. Longer pre-delay keeps a vocal or dialogue line clear of its reverb, and makes a space feel larger without a longer tail.

Early reflections, roughly the first 50 to 80 ms, tell the ear about the size and shape of the space and the source's position in it. Decay time is usually given as RT60, the time for the tail to fall by 60 dB. Damping makes high frequencies die away faster than low ones, as air and soft surfaces do in real rooms. More damping gives a darker, more natural tail that sits behind the mix. Many reverbs also have a bass multiplier for the decay at low frequencies. Diffusion sets how quickly the echoes blur into a smooth tail.

A feedback delay sends part of its output back to its input. With feedback gain g, each repeat is 20·log10(g) dB below the last. At 50% (g = 0.5) each repeat is about 6 dB down, so it takes about 10 repeats to fall 60 dB. With a 375 ms delay that is about 3.7 s. Gain at or above 1 never decays and runs away. Short delays with feedback form a feedback comb filter with resonant peaks every 1/t Hz. A 5 ms loop rings at 200, 400, 600 Hz and so on, which is the metallic tone of flanging and of a badly tuned reverb. Algorithmic reverbs avoid this by mixing many such loops of unrelated lengths, as in Schroeder designs and feedback delay networks.

In practice, set the pre-delay first, then the decay, then the damping. For music, delay times are often set to tempo: a quarter note at 100 BPM is 600 ms. In post, match a reverb to the location by its early reflections and decay, and use damping so ADR sits with production dialogue. Live, keep reverb tails short in reverberant venues, because the room adds its own decay.
keyPoints: Pre-delay: gap before the reverb; about 2.9 ms per metre of extra path.
Early reflections give size, shape and position cues.
RT60 is the time for the tail to fall by 60 dB.
Damping shortens the high-frequency decay.
Each repeat falls by 20·log10(g) dB; g = 0.5 gives about 6 dB per repeat.
A short feedback loop rings at multiples of 1/t.
sayIt: The gap before the reverb lets your voice speak clearly first, and then the space blooms behind it.
inPractice: On a dry vocal, set a plate to 2 s decay and sweep the pre-delay from 0 to 60 ms. Note where the words stay clear but the space still feels joined to the voice, then adjust the damping until the tail stops competing with the consonants.
mistake: People often lengthen the decay to make a space sound bigger, and the mix turns muddy. Pre-delay and early reflections convey size more cleanly; keep the tail only as long as the tempo or scene allows.

terms.def: The time between the direct sound and the start of the reverb.
The first distinct reflections, roughly within 50–80 ms, which give cues about the size and shape of a space.
The time it takes for the reverb tail to decay by 60 dB.
A control that makes high frequencies decay faster than low frequencies.
The part of a delay's output fed back to its input, which sets how many repeats you hear.
In concert-hall acoustics, the time between the direct sound and the first reflection.

title: Dolby Atmos: beds, objects and re-renders
summary: Dolby Atmos mixes combine beds, which are channel-based stems tied to fixed speaker positions, with objects, which are audio plus position metadata. A renderer turns both into speaker feeds or a binaural headphone signal at playback, so one master can play on many speaker layouts.
body:
A bed is a channel-based stem, up to 7.1.2: L, R, C, LFE, two side surrounds, two rear surrounds and two top surrounds. Each bed channel goes to a fixed place. Beds suit ambiences, music stems and anything you would mix in channels anyway. The LFE channel exists only in a bed. An object is a mono signal with metadata, mainly X, Y and Z position and size. It has no fixed speaker. The renderer works out which speakers play it, based on the layout in the room.

The Dolby Atmos Renderer accepts 128 inputs. A typical session uses one 7.1.2 bed (10 channels), which leaves 118 objects. Every extra bed costs inputs: two 7.1.2 beds leave 108. Dialogue is often kept as objects or in the bed centre, depending on the facility and the deliverable. Because the speaker feeds are computed at playback, the same master plays on 7.1.4, 9.1.6 or a soundbar. The master is delivered as an ADM BWF file or a Dolby Atmos master file set. Consumer codecs such as Dolby Digital Plus with Joint Object Coding use spatial coding, which groups objects into a smaller number of elements.

Headphones get a binaural render. Each object has a binaural render mode: Off, Near, Mid or Far. This setting only changes the headphone render. It does nothing to speaker playback. Near keeps a sound close to the head; Far adds more distance and room. Check the binaural render on real headphones, because many listeners will hear the mix that way.

The renderer can also make channel-based re-renders, such as 7.1, 5.1 and 2.0. Trim and downmix controls set how heights and surrounds fold into smaller layouts. A standard Lo/Ro stereo downmix (ITU-R BS.775) adds the centre and surrounds to left and right at −3 dB. Lt/Rt instead matrix-encodes surround information for a decoder. Re-renders are where problems appear: dialogue masked by folded-down effects, phasey height content, or a loudness change. Listen to every re-render you deliver and measure its loudness separately.
keyPoints: Bed = channels at fixed positions, up to 7.1.2; object = mono audio + position metadata.
Renderer: 128 inputs. One 7.1.2 bed (10 ch) leaves 118 objects.
LFE exists only in a bed; objects have no LFE send.
Binaural render mode (Off/Near/Mid/Far) affects headphones only.
Re-renders (5.1, 2.0) depend on trim and downmix settings: always listen to them.
Lo/Ro stereo adds centre and surrounds at −3 dB.
sayIt: In Atmos, some sounds are locked to channels and others carry their own position, so the same mix adapts to cinemas, living rooms and headphones.
inPractice: On your next Atmos mix, solo the 2.0 re-render for a dialogue-heavy scene and compare it with the 7.1.4 playback. Note where effects mask speech and adjust the trims or the object balance, then re-measure loudness on each deliverable.
mistake: Assuming the binaural setting also changes the speaker mix. It only changes the headphone render, so judge Near/Mid/Far on headphones, not on the room speakers.

terms.def: Channel-based stem (up to 7.1.2) with each channel tied to a fixed speaker position.
Mono audio plus metadata (position, size) that the renderer places at playback.
Software or hardware that turns beds and object metadata into speaker or headphone feeds.
A channel-based version (e.g. 5.1, 2.0) generated from the Atmos mix.
Broadcast WAV file carrying audio plus Audio Definition Model metadata; a common Atmos master format.

title: Cardioid sub arrays and end-fire
summary: Subwoofers are almost omnidirectional, so arrays use spacing, delay and sometimes polarity inversion to add in front and cancel behind. The two common forms are the gradient (cardioid) pair and the end-fire line.
body:
A single sub radiates nearly equally in all directions, because its wavelengths are much larger than the box. To steer it you need more than one source. You set delay and polarity so the sources add in one direction and cancel in another. All the maths comes from path difference: sound travels about 0.343 m per millisecond, so a spacing d corresponds to a time of d/c.

In a gradient pair, a rear sub sits a distance d behind the front sub, with its polarity reversed and a delay of d/c. Behind the array, the front sub's sound has to travel the extra distance d, so it arrives at the same moment as the delayed rear sub. Equal level and opposite polarity cancel. In front, the rear sub's sound arrives 2d/c late and inverted. At the frequency where d is a quarter wavelength, that delay is half a period, so the inversion turns it back into addition: about +6 dB. At low frequencies the front sum falls, so gradient arrays usually need EQ. Where d is half a wavelength, the front sum cancels. With d = 0.86 m that happens near 200 Hz, usually above the sub band.

In an end-fire line, all subs face the audience with normal polarity. They are spaced along the throw axis, often around 1 m, and each sub further forward is delayed by d/c relative to the one behind it. In front, every wavefront arrives together and adds. Behind, adjacent subs arrive 2d/c apart, so the sum cancels at some frequencies and only partly at others. For two subs, the deepest rear cancellation is where 2d is half a wavelength, f = c/4d: about 86 Hz for 1 m. More elements widen the rear rejection range.

In practice, rear rejection is never perfect across the whole band. It depends on matched boxes, accurate delays and temperature. Measure behind the array, at the stage or the mix position, and check the front response at the audience. Cardioid subs reduce low-frequency build-up on stage and help keep the low end out of microphones and monitors.
keyPoints: Delay per metre: d/c, about 2.92 ms per metre at 343 m/s.
Gradient pair: rear sub inverted and delayed by d/c; cancels behind.
End-fire: all same polarity, each forward sub delayed by d/c; adds in front.
Two-element end-fire rear null: f = c/4d (≈86 Hz at 1 m).
Rejection is frequency-dependent: always measure front and back.
sayIt: We arrange and delay the subs so the bass adds up towards the audience and cancels on stage, which keeps the stage cleaner and the mix tighter.
inPractice: When you set up a two-box end-fire, set the front box delay to spacing ÷ 343 in milliseconds, then measure with a mic 5 m behind and 5 m in front. Note the frequency of the deepest rear null and compare it with c/4d.
mistake: Thinking end-fire needs a polarity flip like a gradient pair. End-fire uses only spacing and delay; the polarity inversion belongs to the gradient (cardioid) arrangement.

terms.def: Front sub plus a rear sub with reversed polarity and delay d/c, cancelling behind.
Subs in a line along the throw axis, delayed so their outputs add in front.
Difference in distance travelled by two sounds; divided by c it gives the time difference.
How much lower the level is behind an array than in front, at a given frequency.

title: RF coordination and intermodulation
summary: When two or more radio transmitters operate near each other, non-linear circuits mix their signals and create new frequencies called intermodulation products. Frequency coordination chooses channels so these products do not land on any frequency in use.
body:
Intermodulation happens in any non-linear stage: transmitter output stages, receiver front ends and amplifiers. Two carriers f1 and f2 produce sums and differences of their multiples. The ones that matter most are the third-order products, 2f1 − f2 and 2f2 − f1. They fall close to the original carriers, inside the same band, so a receiver cannot filter them out. With three or more transmitters you also get three-transmitter products such as f1 + f2 − f3. Fifth-order products, such as 3f1 − 2f2, are weaker but can still matter in a crowded plan.

The arithmetic is simple. If f1 = 550.000 MHz and f2 = 550.400 MHz, the third-order products sit at 549.600 and 550.800 MHz. That is one spacing below and one spacing above the pair. This leads to an important rule: equally spaced channels clash. With 600.0, 600.5 and 601.0 MHz, 2 × 600.5 − 600.0 = 601.0 MHz, which lands right on the third carrier. The number of products grows fast. N transmitters give N(N − 1) two-transmitter third-order products, so 4 transmitters give 12 and 10 transmitters give 90.

Third-order products also rise faster than the signals that create them. In the ideal model, a 1 dB increase in both carriers raises the third-order products by 3 dB. That is why transmitter power, distance between transmitters and gain staging matter. Bodypacks touching each other in a rack or on a costume rail produce strong products. In-ear monitor transmitters are high-power and run continuously, so they are a classic source. Combine them through a proper combiner and keep their antennas apart from receive antennas.

In practice, use coordination software or the manufacturer's tools, which calculate the products and check them against your channels and a scan of the venue. In the EU, the UHF TV band now ends at 694 MHz after the 700 MHz band was reassigned to mobile services, so available space is tighter. Licensing and allowed frequencies are set nationally, so check the rules where you work. Always scan the venue first, then coordinate, then do a walk test with every transmitter on.
keyPoints: Third-order IMD: 2f1 − f2 and 2f2 − f1, close to the carriers.
Equally spaced channels put IMD products on other carriers.
N transmitters → N(N − 1) two-transmitter third-order products.
1 dB more drive → about 3 dB more third-order product.
Separate transmitters, combine IEMs, scan and walk-test.
sayIt: Radio mics can create interference between themselves, so we plan the frequencies as a set and test them all running together before the show.
inPractice: Before your next multi-channel job, take your planned frequencies and calculate 2f1 − f2 and 2f2 − f1 for each pair by hand or in a spreadsheet. Compare the result with your coordination software, then walk-test with all transmitters and IEMs on.
mistake: Picking channels with neat, equal spacing because it looks tidy. Equal spacing guarantees third-order products land on other channels; coordinated plans look irregular for a reason.

terms.def: New frequencies created when two or more signals pass through a non-linear stage.
IMD product such as 2f1 − f2; strong and close to the carriers.
Choosing a set of channels so no IMD product or outside signal lands on a channel in use.
Device that joins several transmitter outputs into one antenna while limiting interaction between them.
Moving a transmitter around the performance area while monitoring receivers for dropouts and noise.

title: Bass traps, absorbers and diffusers
summary: Porous absorbers turn sound into heat as air moves through them, so they work where particle velocity is high. Pressure-based traps work where pressure is high, and diffusers scatter sound instead of absorbing it.
body:
A porous absorber, such as mineral wool or open-cell foam, works by friction. Air particles move through the fibres and lose energy as heat. At a rigid wall the air cannot move, so particle velocity is zero there and pressure is at its maximum. Velocity reaches its first maximum a quarter wavelength from the wall. This is the quarter-wavelength rule: a porous absorber works well down to roughly the frequency whose quarter wavelength equals its depth from the wall. A 0.20 m depth (material plus air gap) reaches λ/4 at about 429 Hz. For 100 Hz, λ/4 is about 0.86 m. Below that frequency absorption falls off gradually rather than stopping.

That is why thin foam tiles control the highs but leave the bass untouched. It is also why spacing a panel off the wall helps: an air gap moves the material towards higher velocity and extends useful absorption lower. Thick porous traps across corners give large depth from both walls. Every room mode has a pressure maximum in the corners, which also makes corners the natural place for pressure-based traps.

Pressure-based traps include membrane (panel) absorbers and Helmholtz resonators. A membrane trap has a sealed air space behind a limp panel. The panel and air spring resonate and absorb a band around their resonant frequency. These traps work best where pressure is high, at boundaries and in corners. They are tuned, so they target a specific problem, such as a strong mode you have measured.

Absorption is given by a coefficient α from 0 (all reflected) to 1 (all absorbed), and it varies with frequency. Diffusers do something different. A quadratic residue diffuser (QRD) has wells whose depths follow s = n² mod N for a prime N; for N = 7 the sequence is 0, 1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1. The wells scatter reflections over many directions, so energy stays in the room but no single strong reflection arrives at the listener. Deeper wells are needed to work at lower frequencies. Measure the room before and after any treatment.
keyPoints: Porous absorbers need particle velocity: max at λ/4 from a wall.
Depth of 0.20 m reaches λ/4 at about 429 Hz; 100 Hz needs about 0.86 m.
Air gaps and thick corner traps extend porous absorption lower.
Membrane and Helmholtz traps work on pressure, best at walls and corners.
Diffusers scatter energy; QRD wells follow n² mod N.
sayIt: Thin panels only tame the treble; to control the bass we need deep traps in the right places, and diffusers to keep the room sounding open.
inPractice: Measure a room's low-frequency response at the listening position, then add thick porous traps across the front corners and measure again. Compare the decay of the strongest modes in a waterfall plot, not just the level.
mistake: Calling thin foam a 'bass trap'. A 5 cm panel flat on a wall barely affects frequencies below a few hundred hertz; low-frequency control needs depth or a tuned pressure trap.

terms.def: Material that absorbs by friction as air moves through it, e.g. mineral wool.
Fraction of incident sound energy absorbed at a given frequency, from 0 to 1.
Panel over a sealed air space that resonates and absorbs a low-frequency band.
Diffuser with well depths set by n² mod N, scattering reflections over many angles.

title: FM and granular synthesis
summary: FM synthesis uses one oscillator to modulate the frequency of another, creating sidebands whose strength depends on the modulation index. Granular synthesis builds sound from many very short, enveloped grains taken from a sample or oscillator.
body:
In FM, a modulator at fm changes the frequency of a carrier at fc. The result has sidebands at fc ± n·fm. The modulation index I = Δf / fm sets how much energy moves into the sidebands, where Δf is the peak frequency deviation. The amplitude of each sideband follows a Bessel function, Jn(I). As the index rises, energy spreads further out and the sound gets brighter. The carrier itself can disappear: J0 is zero at an index of about 2.405. Carson's rule estimates the bandwidth as 2(Δf + fm). With fm = 200 Hz and Δf = 600 Hz, that is about 1600 Hz.

The carrier-to-modulator ratio (C:M) sets the type of spectrum. Simple integer ratios such as 1:1 or 1:2 give harmonic spectra. Sidebands below 0 Hz fold back as positive frequencies with inverted phase, which also lands on harmonics with integer ratios. Non-integer ratios, such as 1:1.414, give inharmonic spectra that suit bells, metal and clangs. John Chowning described the technique in 1973. Yamaha's DX7 used six operators arranged in 32 algorithms; in practice its oscillators use phase modulation, which behaves very much like FM. Envelopes on the modulator levels make the brightness change over time, which is the key to expressive FM sounds.

Granular synthesis cuts a source into grains, usually between about 1 and 100 ms long. Each grain gets a smooth window, such as a Gaussian or Hann shape, to avoid clicks. The main controls are grain size, density (grains per second), read position, pitch and random spread (jitter) on these values. Overlap is size times density: 50 ms grains at 40 per second give an average of two grains at once. At low density you hear separate particles; at high density they fuse into a continuous texture.

Because read position and grain pitch are independent, granular methods can stretch time without changing pitch, or change pitch without changing duration. Freezing the read position turns one moment of a recording into a sustained pad. In sound design this gives ambiences, risers and tonal beds from production sound or effects, while staying connected to the original source.
keyPoints: FM sidebands at fc ± n·fm; strength set by Bessel functions of I.
Index I = Δf / fm; more index, brighter sound.
Carson's rule: bandwidth ≈ 2(Δf + fm).
Integer C:M → harmonic; non-integer → inharmonic (bells).
Grains about 1–100 ms, windowed; overlap = size × density.
Granular separates time from pitch.
sayIt: FM gets complex tones from just a few oscillators, and granular rebuilds a recording from tiny slices so we can stretch or freeze it without changing its pitch.
inPractice: Take a 3-second production effect, load it into a granular instrument and freeze the read position on its most interesting moment. Then raise density until the grains fuse, and add a little position jitter to build a usable ambience bed.
mistake: Thinking the modulator frequency alone sets FM brightness. Brightness is mainly set by the index (deviation relative to fm); the ratio sets where the partials fall.

terms.def: The oscillator you hear, whose frequency is being modulated.
The oscillator that varies the carrier's frequency.
Peak frequency deviation divided by the modulator frequency.
A very short, windowed slice of sound, usually about 1–100 ms.
Number of grains started per second.

title: Backups, naming and session handover
summary: Good practice means keeping several independent copies of your work, naming files so anyone can find and sort them, and handing over sessions with enough documentation that someone else can open and finish them. The 3-2-1 rule is the usual baseline for backups.
body:
The 3-2-1 rule says: keep three copies of your data, on two different types of storage, with one copy off site. A drive failure, a theft, a fire or a ransomware attack should never destroy every copy. A RAID mirror is not a backup: it protects against one disk failing, but a deletion or corruption is mirrored instantly. The same is true of simple cloud sync. If you delete a folder, the sync service deletes it everywhere. You need versioning or a separate backup that keeps older states.

A copy is only useful if it is correct. On location and in post, verify copies with checksums such as MD5 or xxHash. The software reads the source and the copy and compares the hashes. Matching hashes show the files are bit-identical; a matching file size does not. Film crews often use offload tools that write a media hash list (MHL) so the next person can check the files again. Test restores from time to time. A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan.

Naming should sort correctly and survive any operating system. Use dates as YYYY-MM-DD (ISO 8601), so alphabetical order is also chronological. Avoid spaces and special characters such as / \ : * ? " < > |, and do not rely on upper versus lower case to tell files apart. Use a clear structure: project, episode or reel, content, version. Write 'v03', not 'final_final2'. On set, name scenes and takes consistently and fill in the metadata, because it travels with the Broadcast WAV files to the editor.

A handover should let someone else open the session without calling you. Include a short document with sample rate, bit depth, frame rate, start timecode, track layout and the software version. List the plugins and print or commit any processed tracks, because the recipient may not own the same plugins. Deliver stems and mixes as agreed, with a sound report or cue sheet where needed. Agree in writing what will be delivered, in which formats, and how long you will keep the archive. Ownership of session files and raw recordings depends on the contract, so make it explicit.
keyPoints: 3-2-1: three copies, two media types, one off site.
RAID and sync are not backups: they copy mistakes too.
Verify copies with checksums, and test restores.
Dates as YYYY-MM-DD; no spaces or special characters; versions as v01, v02.
Handover notes: rates, timecode, plugins, printed tracks, deliverables list.
sayIt: Your project is stored in three places, one of them off site, and every handover comes with notes so anyone can open it.
inPractice: At the end of your next session, copy the project to two other destinations, one off site, and verify one copy with checksums. Then write a one-page handover note listing sample rate, frame rate, start timecode, plugins and printed stems.
mistake: Treating a RAID array or a synced cloud folder as a backup. Both copy deletions and corruption immediately; a real backup keeps independent, versioned copies.

terms.def: Three copies of data, on two different types of storage, with one copy off site.
A short value calculated from a file's content; matching values show two copies are identical.
Date written as YYYY-MM-DD, which sorts correctly as text.
A file recording checksums of offloaded media so later copies can be verified.
A submix of related elements (e.g. dialogue, music, effects) delivered as its own file.
